Abd ibn Humayd ibn Abdullah ibn Ubaydah narrated something similar. Likewise, Abu Dawud in his Naskh, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated something similar from Al-Suddi. Abd ibn Humayd, Abu Dawud in his Naskh and Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Qatadah, who said: The Arabs had no religion, so they were forced to accept their religion by the sword. He said: Do not force the Jews, Christians or Magians if they pay the jizyah. Saeed ibn Mansur narrated something similar from Al-Hasan. Al-Bukhari narrated on the authority of Aslam: I heard Umar ibn al-Khattab say to an old Christian woman: Convert to Islam and you will be safe. She refused, so he said: O God, bear witness. Then he recited: There is no compulsion in religion. Saeed ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority that he said to his slave Zanbaq al-Rumi: If you convert to Islam, I will be satisfied with you as a trustee of the Muslims. He refused, so he said: There is no compulsion in religion. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Sulayman ibn Musa regarding his statement: There is no compulsion in religion, he said: It was abrogated by: Fight the disbelievers and the hypocrites. Saeed ibn Mansur, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: Taghut is the devil. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ikrimah, who said: Taghut is the soothsayer. Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Abu al-Aaliyah, who said: Taghut is the magician. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Malik ibn Anas, who said: Taghut is that which is worshipped besides God. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: The firmest handhold is there is no god but God. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Anas bin Malik that it is the Qur’an. Abd bin Hamid, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Mujahid that it is faith. Sufyan narrated that it is the word of sincerity. It has been proven in the two Sahihs that the interpretation of the firmest handhold in other verses is Islam, with a chain of transmission traceable to the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) in his interpretation of the dream of Abdullah bin Salam. Ibn Asakir narrated on the authority of Abu Al-Darda’ that he said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said: “Follow the example of those who come after me, Abu Bakr and Umar, for they are the extended rope of God. Whoever holds fast to them has held fast to the firmest handhold of God that will never break.” Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he said: If one believes in the Oneness of God and in predestination, then it is the firmest handhold. Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Muadh that he was asked about the statement: It will never break. He said: It will never be interrupted before entering Paradise. Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: God is the ally of those who believe verse, he said: They are people who disbelieved in Jesus and then believed in Muhammad (peace be upon him). Those who disbelieve, their allies are false gods verse, he said: They are people who believed in Jesus and then when Muhammad was sent, they disbelieved in him. Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of al-Dahhak who said: Darkness is disbelief. And light is faith. Abu al-Shaykh narrated something similar on the authority of al-Suddi.
2:258: In this verse there is evidence for what was mentioned above that the infidels' allies are the tyrant, and the question mark is to deny the negation and confirm the negated: that is, has your knowledge or insight not ended with the one from whom this argument came? Al-Farra' said: Have you not seen means have you seen: that is, have you seen the one who argued with Abraham, who is Nimrod bin Kus bin Canaan bin Salm bin Noah, and it was said that he is Nimrod bin Falakh bin Amir bin Shalikh bin Arfakhshad bin Sam. And his statement: 258- that God gave him the kingdom means because God gave him, or because God gave him the meaning that giving him the kingdom made him arrogant and caused him to become proud and stubborn, so he argued for that, or that he placed the argument, which is the ugliest form of disbelief, in the place of what is due from him of gratitude, as one says: you were hostile to me because I was good to you, or when God gave him the kingdom. His saying: When Abraham said is an adverb for Hajj, and it was said: instead of his saying: That God gave him the kingdom in the last way, which is far-fetched. His saying: My Lord is He who gives life and causes death with the opening of the ya of my Lord, and it was read without it. His saying: I give life The majority of the reciters read I give life by dropping the alif after the nun from I in the connection, and Nafi’ and Ibn Abi Uways confirmed it as in the saying of the poet: I am the chief of the tribe, so know me as Hamid, the one with the most prominent hump. Abraham, peace be upon him, wanted to say that God is the One who creates life and death in bodies, and the disbeliever wanted to say that He is able to forgive killing, so that would be life, and to kill, so that would be death. This was a foolish answer that cannot be used in response to Abraham’s argument, because he wanted something other than what the disbeliever wanted. If he had said to him: My Lord, who creates life and death in bodies, are You able to do that? the disbeliever would have been dumbfounded at the beginning and at first glance. But he moved with him to another argument to relieve his suffocation and to unleash the reins of debate, so he said: For God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west, because this argument does not involve sophistry and it is not easy for the disbeliever to get out of it by way of stubbornness and quarrel. His saying: Then the one who disbelieved was dumbfounded The man was dumbfounded, dumbfounded, and dumbfounded: if he stopped and was silent, perplexed. Ibn Jarir said: It was narrated from some Arabs in this meaning that he was dumbfounded with the opening of the ba’ and the ha’. Ibn Jinni said: Abu Haywah read Fabahat with a fatha on the ba’ and a damma on the ha’, which is a variant of Baht with a kasra on the ha’. He said: Ibn al-Sameefa’ read Fabahat with a fatha on the ba’ and the ha’, meaning Fabahat Ibrahim who disbelieved, so alladhi is in the accusative case. He said: It is possible that Baht with a fatha on both of them is a variant of Baht. Abu al-Hasan al-Akhfash reported a reading of Fabahat with a kasra on the ha’. He said: And most of them are with a fatha on the ha’. Ibn Atiyyah said: Some people interpreted the reading of those who read Fabahat with a fatha on both of them as meaning cursing and slandering, and that Nimrod was the one who cursed when he was cut off and had no way out. And God the Almighty said: So the one who disbelieved was confounded, and He did not say Fabahat who argued, indicating that that argument was disbelief. And His statement: And God does not guide the wrongdoing people is a conclusion confirming the meaning of the sentence before it. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ali ibn Abi Talib that the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord was Nimrod ibn Canaan. Ibn Jarir narrated it on the authority of Mujahid, Qatadah, Ar-Rabi’ and As-Suddi. Abd Al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Al-Shaykh in Al-Azmah narrated on the authority of Zayd ibn Aslam: The first tyrant on earth was Nimrod, and people used to go out to buy food from him. Abraham, peace be upon him, went out to buy food with those who bought it. When people passed by him, he would say: Who is your Lord? They said: You. Then Abraham passed by him and he said: Who is your Lord? He said: He is the One who gives life and causes death. He said: I give life and cause death. He said: God brings the sun from the east, so bring it from the west. So the disbeliever was dumbfounded, so he sent him back without food. So Abraham returned to his family and passed by a yellow sand dune and said, Shall I not take some of this and bring it to my family, so that they may be pleased when I enter upon them? So he took some of it and went to his family, put down his belongings and went to sleep. His wife went to his belongings and opened them and there was the best food he had ever seen. She made him some of it and brought it to him, for he had known his family had no food with them. He said, Where is this from? She said, It is from the food that you have brought. He knew that God had provided for him, so he praised God. Then God sent an angel to the tyrant, saying, Believe me and leave you in your kingdom. He said, Is there a lord other than me? Then he came to him a second time and said that to him, but he refused. Then he came to him a third time and he refused. Then the king said to him: Gather your armies for three days. So the tyrant gathered his armies, and God commanded the king to open a gate of mosquitoes upon him. The sun rose and they did not see it in great numbers. Then God sent mosquitoes upon them and they ate their fat and drank their blood, leaving nothing but bones, and the king remained as he was, nothing of that affected him. Then God sent a mosquito upon him and it entered his nostril. He remained for four hundred years hitting his head with hammers. The most merciful of people to him was the one who gathered his hands and then hit his head with them. He was a tyrant for four hundred years, so God tormented him for four hundred years as his kingdom was, then God caused him to die. He was the one who had built a tower reaching the sky, so God destroyed its structures from the foundations. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding the verse, saying: He is Nimrod ibn Canaan. They claim that he was the first king on earth. He came with two men, killed one of them and left the other, and said: I give life and cause death. Abu Sheikh narrated on the authority of Al-Suddi: And God does not guide the wrongdoing people. He said: To faith.
2:259: His saying: 259- "Or like the one" or for conjunction based on the meaning, and the estimate: Have you seen like the one who argued or like the one who passed by a village? Al-Kisa'i and Al-Farra' said it. Al-Mubarrad said: The meaning is: Have you not seen the one who argued with Abraham about his Lord, have you not seen who is like the one who passed by a village? So he omitted his saying who is he? A group chose that the kaf is redundant, and others chose that it is nominal. The famous view is that the village is Jerusalem after Bukhtanasr destroyed it, and it was said: What is meant by the village is its people. And his saying: "Empty on its thrones" means fallen on its thrones, meaning the roof fell and then the walls fell on it, Al-Suddi said it and Ibn Jarir chose it, and it was said: Its meaning is empty of people and the houses are standing, and the origin of emptiness is emptiness, it is said: the house became empty and emptied and emptied and emptied: it became deserted, and emptiness is also hunger due to the stomach being empty of food. The first statement is apparent, based on the meaning of his statement: "on its thrones from the word khawa the house collapsed or from khawat" the earth collapsed and this sentence is a circumstantial statement: that is, from the state of being like that. And his statement: "How will God revive this?" means when will He revive or how will He revive, and this is a ruling out of reviving it while it is in that state similar to the state of the dead that is different from the state of the living, and the object is presented because the ruling out arises from his side and not from the side of the agent. So when the passerby said this statement ruling out reviving the mentioned village by populating it and dwelling in it, God gave him an example in himself of something greater than what he asked about, "So God caused him to die for a hundred years and then resurrected him." At-Tabari narrated from some of them that he said: This statement was a doubt in the ability of God, the Most High, to revive a village by bringing it to life, and doubt can only be imagined if his question was about reviving its dead. And his statement: "a hundred years" is an accusative of circumstance. And the year: the year is originally a source like the year, and this amount of time is named after it. His saying: He resurrected him means He revived him. His saying: He said, ‘How long have you remained?’ is a resumption, as if someone asked him what he said to him after his resurrection. There is disagreement about the subject of said. It was said: It is God, the Almighty, and it was said: The angel of the heavens called him with that. It was said: It is Gabriel, and it was said: Someone else. It was said: It is a prophet from the prophets. It was said: A man from the believers from his people who witnessed him with him that God caused him to die and he lived until his resurrection. The first is more appropriate because of his saying later: And look at the bones, how We raise them up. Ibn Amir and the people of Kufa, except for Asim, read: How long have you remained? by assimilating the tha’ into the ta’. And "kam" is in the accusative case as an adverbial phrase, and he only said: "a day or part of a day" based on what he had and thought, so he would not be lying. Similar to this is the statement of the People of al-Kahf 18:"They said, 'We stayed a day or part of a day'" and similar to this is the statement of the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) in the story of Dhu al-Yadayn: "You did not fall short, nor did I forget." This is what supports the statement of those who said: Truth is that which matches belief, and falsehood is that which contradicts it. And his statement: "He said, 'Rather, I stayed a hundred years'" is also a resumption as mentioned previously: meaning, I did not stay a day or part of a day, rather I stayed a hundred years. And his statement: "Then look at your food and your drink; it has not become stale" is God's command to look at this great effect of the effects of power, which is the lack of change in his food and drink despite the length of that period. Ibn Mas'ud read: "This is your food and your drink, it has not become stale" and Talha ibn Musarraf read: "Look at your food and your drink for a hundred years." It was also narrated from Talha that he read: "It has not become stale" by assimilating the ta' into the seen and deleting the ha'. The majority of people read it with the ha’ in the connection, and tasna is taken from as-sunnah: meaning the years did not change it, and its origin is sanah or sanwah from sanahat an-nakhlah and tasnahat: if the years came upon it, and a palm tree sanaa: meaning it bears one year and does not bear another, and asnahat at the Banu Fulan: I stayed with them, and its origin is yatasana, the alif was dropped for the jazm and the ha’ for the sukun. It was said: it is from asna al-ma’: if it changed, and based on this it should have been said: yatasna from his saying: al-hama masnoon said by Abu Amr al-Shibanis. Al-Zajjaj said: it is not like that, because his saying: al-masnoon does not mean it changed, but rather it means it was poured on the age of the earth. And his saying: And look at your donkey the commentators differed in its meaning, the majority went to that its meaning is look at it how its parts were scattered, and its bones decayed, then God revived it and it returned as it was. Ad-Dahhak and Wahb ibn Munabbih said: Look at your donkey standing in its stable, nothing has happened to it after a hundred years have passed. The first statement is supported by the Almighty’s statement: And look at the bones - how We raise them up. The second statement is supported by its relevance to His statement: Then look at your food and your drink - it has not become stale. Rather, the Almighty mentioned that his food and drink did not change after informing him that he had remained for a hundred years, although the fact that that food and drink did not change is not suitable as evidence for that long period. Rather, what He said about his remaining for a day or part of a day is to increase the greatness of that which God caused to die for that period. For if he saw that his food and drink did not change, although he thought that he had only remained for a day or part of a day, his confusion would increase and his doubt would become stronger. So if he looked at his donkey’s rotten bones, he would decide that this was the work of One whose power is beyond the comprehension of the minds, for the food and drink are happy to change. And they remained unchanged for this long period, and the donkey lives for a long period. And it became like this So blessed be God, the best of creators. His saying: "And We will make you a sign for the people." Al-Farra' said: He inserted the waw in his saying: "And We will make you" to indicate that it is a condition for a verb after it, meaning: And We will make you a sign for the people and an indication of the resurrection after death, We made that. If you wish, you can make the waw an inserted and redundant word. Al-A'mash said: The place where it is a sign is that he came as a young man in the same state as he was on the day he died, and he found his sons and grandsons old. His saying: "And look at the bones, how We raise them." The Kufians and Ibn Amir read it with a zay, and the rest read it with a ra'. Abaan narrated from Asim Nasha'ra with a fatha on the first noon and a sukoon on the second, and a damma on the sheen and the ra'. Al-Hakim narrated and authenticated it from Zayd ibn Thabit that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, read Kayfa nanshazha with a zay. So the meaning of reading with a zay is that we raise it, and from it comes the nashz: which is the elevated part of the earth, meaning that some of it is raised to others. As for the meaning of reading with the silent ra’, it is clear from God resurrected the dead: meaning He brought them back to life. And His statement: Then We clothed them with flesh: meaning: We covered them with it as we cover the body with clothing. So clothing was used as a metaphor for that, just as al-Nabigha used a metaphor for Islam, saying: Praise be to God that my death did not come until I had put on a garment of Islam. His statement: When it became clear to him meaning what was mentioned previously of the signs that God Almighty showed him and commanded him to look at and ponder, he said, ‘I know that God has power over all things’ nothing is impossible for Him. Ibn Jarir said: The meaning of his statement: When it became clear to him is when what was strange about God’s power became clear to him clearly before he saw it. He said, ‘I know.’ Abu Ali al-Farisi said that it means: I know that this is the kind of knowledge that I did not know. Hamza and al-Kisa’i read They said, ‘Your Lord knows best’ in the form of a command, addressing himself in a manner of abstraction. Abd bin Hamid, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated, and authenticated it, on the authority of Ali, regarding his statement: Or like the one who passed by a town, he said: Uzair, the Prophet of God, left his city when he was a young man, and passed by a ruined town, which was empty of its inhabitants, and said: How can God revive this after its death? So God caused him to die for a hundred years, then He resurrected him. The first thing God created were his eyes, and he began to look at his bones as they joined together, then they were covered with flesh, then the soul was breathed into him. It was said to him: How long did you stay? He said: I stayed a day or part of a day. He said: Rather, I stayed a hundred years. So he came to his city. He had left behind a young cobbler neighbor, and he came back when he was an old man. It was narrated from a group of the Salaf that the one whom God caused to die was Ezra, among them Ibn Abbas according to Ibn Jarir and Ibn Asakir, and among them Abdullah bin Salam according to Al-Khatib and Ibn Asakir, and among them Ikrimah, Qatadah, Sulayman, Buraydah, Ad-Dahhak and As-Suddi according to Ibn Jarir, and it was narrated from another group that the one whom God caused to die was a prophet named Jeremiah, among them Abdullah bin Ubayd bin Umair according to Abd bin Hamid, Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim, and among them Wahb bin Munabbih according to Abd Al-Razzaq, Ibn Jarir and Abu Al-Shaykh. Ibn Ishaq also narrated from him that he was Al-Khidr. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from a man from the people of Ash-Sham that he was Ezekiel. Ibn Kathir narrated from Mujahid that he was a man from the Children of Israel. The first opinion is more popular. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: khawiya he said: ruins. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah who said: khawiya with no one in it. He also narrated from Ad-Dahhak who said: on its roofs its ceilings. Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Al-Suddi who said: It fell on its roofs. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Qatada who said: It stayed for a day, then he turned and saw the sun and said: Or part of a day. He also narrated on his authority who said: The food that he had with him was a basket of figs, and his drink was a skin of juice. He also narrated something similar on the authority of Mujahid. Abu Ya’la, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: It has not become stale, he said: It has not changed. Abd bin Hamid and Ibn Jarir narrated that: It has not become stale, he said: It has not become foul. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Mas’ud regarding his statement: And We will make you a sign to the people, something similar to what was mentioned above on the authority of Al-A’mash, and he also narrated something similar on the authority of Ikrimah. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: How shall We raise it up? he said: We shall bring it out. Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Zaid bin Thabit who said: We shall revive it.
2:260: His saying: 260- And when is an adverb in the accusative case with an omitted verb: i.e. remember the time of Abraham's saying, and the command to remember was directed to the time rather than what happened in it, even though it was the intended purpose, for the purpose of exaggeration, because seeking the time of something necessitates seeking it first, and this is what is said in all the places mentioned in the Noble Book, representing this adverb. And his saying: My Lord he preferred it over others because of what it contains of sympathy that necessitates the acceptance of what comes after it of supplication. And his saying: Show me, Al-Akhfash said: He did not mean seeing with the heart, but rather he meant seeing with the eyes, and others said the same, and it is not correct to mean seeing with the heart here, because Abraham's purpose was to witness the revival so that he would attain tranquility, and the hamza that entered the verb is for the purpose of making it transitive to the second object, which is the sentence: I mean his saying: How do You revive the dead? And how is in the accusative case as a likeness to the adverb or the state, and the agent in it is the verb that comes after it. His saying: Have you not believed? is in apposition to something understood, meaning, have you not known and believed that I am able to bring people back to life so that you ask Me to show them? “He said: Yes.” I knew and believed that You are able to do that, but I asked so that my heart would be reassured by the evidence of seeing things and the evidence of faith. The majority of scholars have said that Abraham never doubted the resurrection of the dead, but rather asked to see things directly because human souls are naturally inclined to see what is reported about them. For this reason, the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said: Hearing is not like seeing things directly. Ibn Jarir narrated from a group of scholars that he asked that because he doubted God’s power. They provided evidence for this with what was authentically reported from him (peace and blessings of God be upon him) in the two Sahihs and others, in his saying: We are more deserving of doubt than Abraham, and with what was narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: There is no verse in the Qur’an that I hope for more than it. It was narrated from him by Abd al-Razzaq, Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it. Ibn Jarir preferred this after narrating it. Ibn Atiyah said: I find it objectionable, meaning the statement of this group. Then he said: As for the statement of the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him): We are more deserving of doubt than Abraham, its meaning is that if he had doubts, we would have been more deserving of him, and we do not doubt, so Abraham is more deserving of not doubting. So the hadith is based on denying doubt from Abraham. As for the statement of Ibn Abbas: It is the most hopeful sign, it is because it contains evidence of God and a request for life in this world, and it is not likely to be so. It is permissible to say that it is the most hopeful sign because of his statement: Have you not believed? meaning that faith is sufficient and does not require investigation and research. He said: So doubt is far from someone who has established his faith only, so how about the status of prophethood and friendship? The prophets are infallible from major and minor sins that include vice by consensus. If you contemplate his question, peace be upon him, and the rest of the words of the verse, you will not be left with any doubt. This is because the question with how is a question about the state of something that exists and is established in the questioner and the one being asked, such as when you say: How did Zaid know? How was the garment woven? And the like. When you say: How is your garment? And how is Zaid? The question is about one of its states. How may be report about something that is supposed to be inquired about with how, such as when you say: How do you wish, then be, and the like of what Al-Bukhari said: How was the beginning of the revelation? In this verse, it is a question about the form of revival, and revival is established. However, when we find that some of those who deny the existence of something may express their denial by asking about the state of that thing, we know that it is not valid. It follows from this that the thing in itself is not valid. An example of this is when a claimant says: I will raise this mountain, and the one who denies him says: Show me how you will raise it. This is a metaphorical way of expression and its meaning is the submission of an argument. The one who denies him says: Show me how to raise it. This is a metaphorical way of expression and its meaning is the submission of an argument, as if he is saying: Suppose you raise it. Since there was this metaphorical ambiguity in the expression of Al-Khalil, God made it clear to him and made him explain the truth to him, so He said to him: Do you not believe? He said: Yes. So the matter was completed and he was freed from everything. Then, peace be upon him, explained his question by saying: Reassurance. Al-Qurtubi said: This is what Ibn Atiyah mentioned and he is an adult. Such doubt is not permissible for the prophets, peace be upon them, because it is disbelief. The prophets agree on belief in the resurrection. God, the Exalted, has informed us that Satan has no way over His prophets and saints. He said: Indeed, you have no authority over My servants. And the accursed one said: Except for Your chosen servants among them. And if he has no authority over them, how can he make you doubt? Rather, he asked to see how the parts of the dead are gathered after they are separated, and the nerves and skins are connected after they are torn apart. So he wanted to ascend from the knowledge of certainty to the eye of certainty. His saying: Show me how is an expression of seeing how. Al-Mawardi said: The alif in his saying: Did you not believe? is not an alif of interrogation, but rather it is an alif of affirmation and confirmation, as Jarir said: Aren't you the best of those who ride mounts and the most generous of the worlds in terms of bellies? The letter waw is the letter waw of state, and you believe: its meaning is absolute faith that includes the virtue of reviving the dead, and tranquility: moderation and calm. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning of for my heart to be reassured is to be certain. His statement: Then take four birds the letter fa is the answer to an omitted condition: that is, if you want that, then take, and the bird: is a collective noun for bird like rakab for rakib, or a collective noun or source, and the bird was singled out for that, it was said: because it is the closest type of animal to man, and it was said: the bird's concern is flying in the sky, and the friend's concern was to rise, and other reasons were said that require the bird to be singled out. All of these do not fatten or satisfy hunger, and they are only the thoughts of the minds and the beginnings of the minds that should not be made faces for the words of God, and reasons for what is mentioned in His words, and so it was said: what is the reason for specifying this number, since tranquility is achieved by reviving one? It was said that Abraham asked for one for the number of servitude, so he was given four for the number of lordship. It was also said that the four birds are a reference to the four pillars from which the pillars of the animal are composed and similar nonsense. His saying: So turn them to you was read with a damma on the sad and a kasra on it: meaning, gather them to you and fold them and gather them. It is said: a man is asawur if his neck is slanted, and it is said that the thing became yasawuruhu: it inclined it. The poet said: God knows that we will look around on the day of separation at our neighbors It was said that its meaning was that he cut them off. It is said: The thing became visible meaning he cut it off. From this is the saying of Tobah bin Al-Humayr: So the reasons brought me closer until I reached it with my rising, and my meeting was depicting it That is, he cuts it off. Based on this, his statement, to you, is connected to his statement, take. His statement, Then place on every mountain a portion of them, contains the command to divide, because placing every portion on a mountain necessitates the precedence of division. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is, then place on every mountain a portion of each one of them, and the portion is the share. His statement, They will come to you, is in the accusative case as an answer to the command, but it was constructed because of the feminine plural nun. His statement, Striving, means to hasten in flying or walking. Ibn Abi Hatim and Abu Al-Sheikh in Al-Azmah narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he said: Abraham passed by a dead man who they claimed was an Ethiopian on the seashore. He saw sea creatures coming out and eating from him, and wild beasts of the earth coming to him and eating from him, and birds landing on him and eating from him. Abraham then said: My Lord, these sea creatures eat from this, and wild beasts of the earth and birds, then you kill these and they decay, then you bring them back to life. Show me how you bring the dead back to life. He said: Do you not believe, O Abraham, that I bring the dead back to life? He said: Yes, O Lord, but so that my heart may be reassured, meaning: so that I may see some of Your signs and know that You have answered me. So God said: Take four birds and do what you have done. The birds that He took were: a goose, a hawk, a rooster, and a peacock. He took two different halves. Then He came to four mountains and made two different halves on each mountain. This is His saying: Then place on each mountain a portion of them. Then he stepped aside and their heads were under his feet. He called upon the Greatest Name of God, and each half returned to its half, and each feather to its bird. Then they came flying without heads to his feet, wanting their heads to their necks. He raised his feet and each bird placed its neck on his head, and they returned as they were. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Qatadah. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir also narrated something similar from al-Hasan. Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Ibn Jurayj that it was the carcass of a donkey. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Al-Bayhaqi narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: but that my heart may be reassured, meaning: I know that You will answer me when I call upon You, and give me when I ask You. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: Then take four of the birds, he said: The crane, the peacock, the rooster, and the pigeon. Abd bin Hamid, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Mujahid, he said: The four of the birds are: The rooster, the peacock, the crow, and the pigeon. Saeed bin Mansour, Abd bin Hamid, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Al-Mundhir, and Al-Bayhaqi narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas: Fasrahenna means: He cut them. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority that he said: It is in Nabataean: He split them. They narrated on his authority that he said: Fasrahenna means: He tied them up. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority that he said: He placed them on seven mountains, and took the heads in his hand and began to look at the drop meeting the drop and the feather meeting the feather until they became alive without heads. Then they came to their heads and entered them.
2:261: His statement: 261- Like a seed It is not correct to make this a predicate of his statement: Like those who spend because they are different, so it is necessary to estimate something omitted. As for the first: meaning like the spending of those who spend, or in the second: meaning like the planter of a seed, and what is meant by the seven ears of corn is what comes out on a single stalk from which seven branches branch out, in each branch is an ear, and the seed is the name for everything that the son of Adam plants, and from it is the saying of Al-Mutalammis: I swear that the love of Iraq will feed me for a lifetime, and that love will eat me in the village of Licorice. It was said: What is meant by ears here are ears of millet, which are those that have this number in an ear. Al-Qurtubi said: An ear of millet comes in an ear more than this number by two times or more, as we have seen. Ibn Atiyyah said: There may be in an ear of wheat what has one hundred grains, but in other grains it is more, but the example was with this amount. Al-Tabari said: His saying: In every ear one hundred grains means if that is found, otherwise it is upon you to impose it. His saying: And God multiplies for whom He wills may mean that He multiplies this multiplication for whom He wills, or He multiplies this number, so He increases it by multiples for whom He wills, and this is the most correct for what will come. The Qur’an has stated that a good deed is worth ten times its like, and this verse requires that the good deed of the expense of jihad is worth seven hundred times, so the general is built on the specific, and this is based on the fact that the path of God is jihad only, but if what is meant by it is the aspects of good, then this multiplication is limited to seven hundred with the reward of the expenses, and the ten times is in everything other than that.
2:262: His statement: 262- Those who spend their wealth in the way of God. This sentence includes an explanation of the manner of spending that was mentioned, i.e. it is the spending of those who spend and then do not follow up what they have spent with a favor or injury. The favor is the mention of the blessing in the sense of enumerating it and rebuking it. It was said that the favor is talking about what was given until it reaches the one who was given and harms him. The favor is one of the major sins as proven in Sahih Muslim and others that it is one of the three whom God will not look at nor purify them and for them is a great punishment. And harm is cursing, arrogance and complaining. It was said in Al-Kashshaf: The meaning of then is to show the difference between spending and leaving the favor and harm, and leaving them is better than spending itself, just as He made steadfastness in faith better than entering into it by His statement: Then they remained steadfast. End. The favor was mentioned for harm because it occurs frequently and the word la is in the middle to indicate the smallness of the negation. His statement: With their Lord contains emphasis and honor. His saying: And there is no fear for them clearly negates fear for them in both worlds, as the indefinite noun in the context of negation indicates comprehensiveness. Likewise, nor will they grieve indicates the continuity of the absence of grief for them.
2:263: His saying: 263- Kindness and forgiveness It was said that the predicate is omitted: meaning better and more appropriate, mentioned by Al-Nahhas. He said: It is permissible for it to be predicate of a deleted subject: meaning what you were commanded to do is a kind word. And his saying: And forgiveness is also a subject and its predicate is his saying: Better than charity. It was said: His saying: better is predicate of his saying: a kind word and of his saying: and forgiveness. It is permissible to begin with the two indefinite nouns because the first is specified by the description, and the second by the conjunction, and the meaning is: that the kind word from the person being asked to the questioner, which is comfort and hope for what is with God, and a good response is better than charity followed by harm. It was proven in Sahih Muslim from him, may God's prayers and peace be upon him: A kind word is charity, and it is from kindness that you meet your brother with a cheerful face. And how beautiful is what Ibn Duraid said: Do not let the one who asks you become bored, for the best thing in your life is to see someone who is asked. Do not answer them with a hopeful face, for the continuation of your glory is to see what is hoped for. What is meant by forgiveness is covering up the faults and the bad condition of the needy, and pardoning the beggar if he is so insistent that it upsets the person being asked. It was said that what is meant is that the pardon is on the part of the beggar, because if he responds to him in a nice way, he will excuse him. It was also said that what is meant is: An action that leads to forgiveness is better than charity: meaning, God’s forgiveness is better than your charity. This sentence is a new sentence that confirms the abandonment of following favors and harm for charity.
2:264: His statement: 264- O you who have believed, do not invalidate your charities with reminders or injury. Invalidating charities: removing their effect and spoiling their benefit: that is, do not invalidate them with reminders or injury or one of them. His statement: like the one who means invalidating like invalidating the one who, as it is an attribute of a deleted source, and it may be a state: that is, do not invalidate, similar to the one who spends his money to be seen by people, and the accusative of showing off is as a reason for his statement: spends meaning for the sake of showing off or a state, that is, he spends showing off, not intending thereby the face of God and the reward of the Hereafter, rather he does that to show off to people, to gain their praise and commendation of him. It was said: What is meant by it is the hypocrite, as evidenced by his statement: and he does not believe in God and the Last Day. His statement: Then his example is like the example of a smooth rock. A smooth rock is a large, smooth stone. Al-Akhfash said: Safwan is the plural of Safwana. Al-Kisa'i said: Safwan is one, and its plural is safy and asfa, but al-Mubarrad denied it. An-Nahhas said: It may be a plural, and it may be a singular, which is more appropriate, because of his statement: There was dust on it, and a downpour struck it. A downpour is a heavy rain. God, the Exalted, likened this spender to a rock on which there was dust, which one would think was good, fertile soil, but when a downpour of rain struck it, the dust was removed from it and it remained solid, i.e., bare and pure of the dust that was on it. Likewise, this hypocrite, for his spending does not benefit him, just as the rain falling on a rock on which there was dust does not benefit. His statement: They are not able to do anything of what they have earned means: They do not benefit from what they did out of hypocrisy, nor do they find any reward for it. The sentence is a new sentence, as if it was said: What will be their state then? So it was said: They are not able, etc. The two pronouns refer to the relative pronouns, i.e. like the one who, according to the meaning, as in His statement, the Exalted: And you plunged like those who plunged meaning the genus, the group, or the plural.
2:265: His saying: 265- And the parable of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God and to strengthen themselves It was said that his saying: Seeking the pleasure of God is an object for it, and strengthening is conjoined to it, and it is also an object for it: meaning spending for the sake of seeking. And strengthening is what Makki said in Al-Mushkil. Ibn Atiyyah said: It is rejected, it is not correct in strengthening that it is an object for the sake of it, because spending is not for the sake of strengthening. He said: And seeking is an accusative of the source in the place of the state, and the accusative of the object for the sake of it would have been directed in it, but the accusative of the source is correct from the aspect of conjoining the source which is strengthening it to it, and seeking means seeking, and satisfaction is a source of contentment, pleases, and strengthening means: that they strengthen themselves by spending their wealth on faith and other acts of worship as exercise for it, training and practice, or strengthening could mean belief: meaning belief in Islam arising from their own selves. The predecessors differed about the meaning of this letter. Al-Hasan and Mujahid said: It means that they are certain to give their charity. It was also said: It means believing and being certain. This was narrated from Ibn Abbas. It was also said: It means that they are counting on themselves. This was said by Qatada. It was also said: It means that their souls have insights, so they make them steadfast in spending in obedience to God. This was said by Al-Sha’bi, Al-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and Abu Salih. This is more correct than the previous one. It is said: He made someone steadfast in this matter. He made his resolve sound. His statement: Like a garden on a hill which is hit by heavy rain. Paradise is the orchard, and it is a land in which trees grow until they cover it. It is taken from the word jinn and fetus because they are hidden. A hill is a slightly elevated place. The letter ra is pronounced with a triangle, and it is read with it. The hill is specifically mentioned because its vegetation is better than others, while it is not usually affected by the cold due to the gentleness of its air when the wind blows gently. Al-Tabari said: It is the gardens of sadness, attributed to Najd. Because it is better than the meadows of Tihamah, and the plants of Najd are more fragrant, and its breeze is cooler and more gentle. Najd is called Hazn, and this mentioned here is not from that, and the word Rabwah is taken from riba yarbu if it increases. Al-Khalil said Rabwah: a high, good land. Al-Waabil is heavy rain as mentioned above, it is said: the sky was wet, and the earth was wet. Al-Akhfash said: And from it is the saying of God the Almighty: A severe seizure meaning severe, and a severe strike, and a severe torment. It brought forth its fruits with a damma on the hamza: the fruit that is eaten, like the saying of God the Almighty: It brings forth its fruits at all times and adding it to Paradise is an addition of specificity like the saddle of a horse and the door of a house. Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu Amr read and its fruits with a damma on the hamza and a sukoon on the kaf for ease. Asim, Ibn Amir, Hamza, and Al-Kisa'i read it with a damma on the kaf. And his saying: double meaning twice what it used to bear because of the rain. What is meant by double is the same, and it was said that it is four times, and its accusative is in the state of eating it: meaning doubled. His statement: And if no downpour hits it, then dew means that dew extinguishes it: and it is the weak rain with a thin drop. Al-Mubarrad and others said: Its meaning is dew that is sufficient for it. Al-Zajjaj said: Its meaning is that what hits it is dew, and what is meant is that dew replaces the downpour in producing the fruit twice. Some people said: Dew is dew. In Al-Sahah, dew is the weakest rain, and the plural is atlal. Al-Mawardi said: And the crops of dew are weaker than the crops of rain. The meaning is that the expenses of these people are pure with God and will not be wasted under any circumstances, even if they vary. It is permissible to consider the analogy between their situation in terms of what they have spent, both a lot and a little, and the promised Paradise in terms of what it has received, both a lot and a little rain. Just as each one of the two rains doubles its food, so too their expenses, whether great or small, after seeking God’s pleasure with them, are pure and increase their reward. And his saying: And God is Seeing of what you do. Al-Zuhri read it with the ta’ below. The majority read it with the ta’ above. In this is an encouragement for them to be sincere, while warning against hypocrisy and the like. It is a promise and a threat. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in his statement: Like a seed that grows seven ears on the authority of Ar-Rabi’ who said: “Whoever pledged allegiance to the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) to emigrate and stayed with him in Madinah and did not go anywhere except with his permission, his reward would be seven hundred times greater. Whoever pledged allegiance to Islam, his reward would be ten times greater.” Muslim, Ahmad, An-Nasa’i, Al-Hakim and Al-Bayhaqi narrated on the authority of Ibn Mas’ud that “a man gave away a bridled camel in charity for the sake of God. The Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said: ‘On the Day of Resurrection, you will have seven hundred bridled camels for it. ’” Ahmad, At-Tirmidhi who classed it as hasan, An-Nasa’i, Ibn Hibban, Al-Hakim who classed it as saheeh and Al-Bayhaqi in Ash-Shu’ab narrated on the authority of Khuzaym ibn Fatik who said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) said: Whoever spends money in the way of God, seven hundred times greater will be recorded for him. Al-Bukhari narrated it in his history from the hadeeth of Anas. Ahmad narrated it from the hadeeth of Abu ‘Ubaidah and added: Whoever spends on himself and his family or visits a sick person, his reward will be ten times greater. An-Nasa’i narrated something similar in his book on fasting. Ibn Majah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from the hadith of Imran bin Husayn, Ali, Abu al-Darda’, Abu Hurayrah, Abu Umamah, Abdullah bin Amr and Jabir, all of them narrating from the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, who said: “Whoever sends money in the cause of God and stays in his house, he will receive seven hundred dirhams on the Day of Resurrection for every dirham. Whoever fights in the cause of God and spends in His cause, he will receive seven hundred thousand dirhams on the Day of Resurrection for every dirham. Then he recited this verse: ‘And God multiplies for whom He wills.’” It was also narrated by Ibn Majah from the hadith of al-Hasan bin Ali. Ahmad narrated from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “Every deed of the son of Adam is multiplied, a good deed by ten times its like, up to seven hundred times, to whatever God wills. God says: Except for fasting, for it is for Me and I will reward for it.” It was also narrated by Muslim. Al-Tabarani narrated from the hadith of Muadh ibn Jabal that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Blessed is he who mentions God a lot in jihad in the way of God, for for every word he says he will have seventy thousand good deeds, each good deed tenfold. Some of the hadiths about multiplying good deeds have already been mentioned in the words of God, the Most High: Who is it that would loan God a goodly loan so He may multiply it for him many times over? There are authentic hadiths about the reward of one who equips a warrior. Abu Dawud and Al-Hakim narrated - and authenticated - on the authority of Sahl ibn Muadh on the authority of his father who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Indeed, prayer, fasting, and remembrance of God are multiplied seven hundred times over spending in the way of God. Ahmad, Al-Tabarani in Al-Awsat, and Al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated on the authority of Buraydah who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Spending in Hajj is like spending in the way of God, seven hundred times. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Al-Hasan, who said in his interpretation of the verse: Then they do not follow up what they have spent with reminders or injury, that some people send a man among them in the cause of God or spend on a man or give him provisions, then he shows him favor and harms him: meaning that this is the reason for the revelation. Abd bin Hamid and Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Qatada something similar. There are authentic hadiths that forbid reminding and harming and the virtue of spending in the cause of God and on relatives and in charitable causes, and there is no need to go on at length by mentioning them as they are well-known in their places. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Amr bin Dinar who said: It has reached us that the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: “There is no charity more beloved to God than speaking the truth. Have you not heard the statement of God, the Most High: ‘A kind word and forgiveness are better than charity followed by injury.’” Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ad-Dahhak regarding the verse: A kind word, he said: A kind response, saying: May God have mercy on you, may God provide for you, and do not scold him or speak harshly to him. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: “A person who shows off will not enter Paradise. This is in the Book of God: ‘Do not invalidate your charities with reminders or injury.’” Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement: a clear rock, he said: and left it bare, meaning: nothing on it. Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ikrimah, who said: the downpour means the rain. They narrated on the authority of Qatada, who said: the downpour means heavy rain. He said: This is a parable that God has given for the deeds of the disbelievers on the Day of al-Qiyamah 75:They will not be able to do anything with what they have earned, on that day, just as this rain left this rock, with nothing on it, purer than it was. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, and left it bare, he said: dry and lying, not growing anything. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ar-Rabi’, regarding his statement: And the example of those who spend their wealth seeking the pleasure of God, he said: This is a parable that God has given for the deeds of the believer. Abd bin Hamid and Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Al-Sha’bi regarding his statement: And to confirm from themselves he said: To confirm and be certain. Ibn Jarir narrated something similar from Abu Salih. Abd bin Hamid and Ibn Jarir narrated: They verify where they put their money. They narrated on the authority of Al-Hasan who said: “When a man intended to give charity, he would confirm it. If God wills, He will carry it out, but if it is mixed with some hypocrisy, he will hold back.” Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Qatadah regarding his statement: To confirm, he said: The intention. Al-Hakim narrated and authenticated it on the authority of Ibn Abbas who said: The high hill is the elevated part of the earth. Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Mujahid who said: The hill is the flat, elevated land. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas who said: It is the elevated place where rivers do not flow. Ibn Jarir narrated on his authority regarding his statement: Dew he said: Dew. Abd bin Hamid and Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Ad-Dahhak who said: Dew is the drizzle of rain, meaning the softness of it. They narrated on the authority of Qatada, who said: This is a parable that God has given for the deeds of the believer, saying: His goodness has no successor, just as the goodness of this Paradise has no successor, no matter what its condition, whether it is hit by rain or dew.
2:266: Love: love for something with wishing for it, and the hamza that enters the verb to deny the occurrence, and Paradise is used for intertwined trees and for the land in which there are trees. The first is more appropriate here because of his saying: 266- Underneath which rivers flow by referring the pronoun back to the trees without the need for a deleted complement. As for the second face, it must be estimated as, from beneath its trees. And so his saying: So it was burned does not need to estimate a complement according to the first face, but as for the second face, it needs to be estimated: that is, its trees were burned, and he specifically mentioned the palm trees and grapes with his saying: For him therein of all kinds of fruits because they are the most generous of trees, and these sentences are attributes of Paradise, and the waw in his saying: And old age afflicted him it was said: is a conjunction with his saying: It will be past tense in future, and it was said with his saying: He wishes and it was said that it is carried on the meaning since it is in the meaning of was and it was said that it is the waw of the state, that is, and old age afflicted him and this is more likely. Old age is a sign of great need, because of the inability of its owner to take the necessary measures. His statement, and he has weak offspring is a state of the pronoun in hit him: meaning, while the case is that he has weak offspring, for whoever combines old age with weak offspring, his regret for that Paradise will be extremely severe. A hurricane is a strong wind that blows from the earth to the sky like a column, and it is what is called a whirlwind, as stated by Al-Zajjaj. Al-Jawhari said: A whirlwind is a chief of the jinn, and from it the hurricane is called a whirlwind. It is also said: Umm Zawba’ah: It is a wind that stirs up dust and rises to the sky like a column. It was also said: It is a wind that stirs up clouds with thunder and lightning. His statement, So it was burned is in apposition to his statement, So it was struck by it. This verse is a representation of someone who does good and adds to it what nullifies it, and then finds it on the Day of Resurrection when he is in great need of it, neither fattening nor satisfying hunger, in the same state as someone who has this described Paradise and is characterized by that characteristic. Al-Bukhari and others narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he said: One day, Umar said to the companions of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, What do you think about this verse, ‘Would any of you like to have Paradise?’ They said: God knows best. He said: “Say: We know or we do not know.” Ibn Abbas said: I have something in my mind about it, O Commander of the Faithful. Umar said: O son of my brother, say it and do not belittle yourself. Ibn Abbas said: You have given an example of a deed. Umar said: What deed? Ibn Abbas said: A rich man who works for the power of God, then God sends Satan to him and he works in sins until his deeds are drowned. Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Umar that he said: This is an example given of a man who does a good deed until, at the end of his life, he is most in need of it, he does a bad deed. Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Hakim narrated, and he authenticated it, through various chains of narration, on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: A whirlwind containing fire. He said: A strong poisonous wind.
2:267: His saying: 267- From the good things that you have earned means: from the good and chosen things that you have earned, this is what the majority said. A group said: The meaning of the good things here is the permissible. There is no objection to considering both matters, because the good and chosen things of earning are only applied to the permissible according to the people of the law, even if the people of the language apply it to what is good in itself, whether it is permissible or forbidden, so the legal reality takes precedence over the linguistic one. And his saying: And from what We have produced for you from the earth means: and from the good things that We have produced for you from the earth, and it was deleted because what preceded it indicates it, which are plants, minerals and treasure. His saying: And do not aim at the bad means: do not aim at the bad money, and the majority read it with the opening of the letter of the present tense and the lightening of the ya, and Ibn Kathir read it with the emphasis. Ibn Masoud read do not aim at it, and it is a language. Abu Muslim bin Khabab read it with the damma of the first letter and the kasra of the meem. Abu Amr narrated that Ibn Masoud read ta’ammu with a hamza after the damma. The verse commands spending good and forbids spending bad. A group of the Salaf believed that the verse is about obligatory charity, while others believed that it includes obligatory and voluntary charity, which is the apparent view. Evidence to support this will come. The presentation of the adverb in His statement, of it you spend indicates specification, meaning do not single out bad money for spending. The sentence is in the accusative case as a state, meaning do not intend bad money, specifying spending with it and restricting it to it. His statement, and you would not take it means: while the situation is that you do not take it in your transactions at any time, this is how the majority explained its meaning. It was said that its meaning is: and you would not take it if you found it being sold in the market. His statement, unless you close your eyes to it is from the verb aghama to close one’s eyes to a man in a matter such and such: if he is lenient and satisfied with some of his right and overlooks it and lowers his gaze from it. From this is the saying of the poet: How many things about you make me anxious, I turn a blind eye to them, I am not blind to them Al-Zuhri read it with a fatha on the ta’ and a kasra on the meem, with a lightened pronunciation. It was narrated from him that he read it with a damma on the ta’ and a fatha on the ghain and a kasra on the meem, with a shaddah. Qatada read it likewise. The meaning according to the first of these two readings is: unless you deprive the seller of its price from you. According to the second reading: unless you take a reduction. Ibn ‘Atiyyah said: The reading of the majority is based on transgression or closing the ‘ayn, because aghmadha is like ghammad, and that it has the meaning of hatta: that is, until you come to something ambiguous in interpretation and consideration of taking that.
2:268: His saying: 268- The devil threatens you with poverty. The meaning of the devil and its derivation have already been mentioned. And he threatens you means he frightens you with poverty: that is, with poverty so that you will not spend. So this verse is connected to what preceded it. And poverty was read with a damma on the fa', which is a language. Al-Jawhari said: And poverty is a language for poverty, like weakness and weakness. And obscenity is the obscene trait, which is sins and spending on them and miserliness in spending on acts of obedience. It was said in Al-Kashshaf: And the obscene among the Arabs is the miser. End. And from it is the saying of Tarafa bin Al-Abd: I see death darkening the honorable and choosing the money of the obscene and extremist Aqila However, even though the Arabs used it to refer to the miser, this does not contradict their using it to refer to other sins, and it has occurred frequently in their speech. And His statement: And God promises you forgiveness from Him and bounty. In the speech of the Arabs, when it is general, it is for good, and when it is restricted, it may sometimes be restricted to good and sometimes to evil. From this is the statement of God the Almighty: The Fire which God has promised to those who disbelieve. And from this is also what is in this verse of restricting the promise of Satan to poverty, and restricting the promise of God the Almighty to forgiveness and bounty. Forgiveness is covering up for His servants in this world and the hereafter for their sins and expiation for them, and bounty is that He replaces for them better than what they spent, so He increases their provisions and bestows upon them in the hereafter what is better, more, more magnificent and more beautiful.
2:269: 269-His saying He is given wisdom is knowledge, and it was said: understanding, and it was said: accuracy in speech, and there is no objection to applying it to all of them comprehensively or alternatively, and it was said: it is prophecy, and it was said: reason, and it was said: fear, and it was said: piety, and the origin of wisdom is that which prevents foolishness, which is every ugly thing. The meaning is: whoever God gives wisdom has given him much good: meaning great in its value and great in its danger. Al-Zuhri and Ya'qub read and whoever is given wisdom in the active form, and the majority read it in the passive form, and the minds: the minds, the singular of which is lab, and we have already discussed it.
2:270: His statement: 270- And whatever you spend “what” is conditional and it may be a relative pronoun, and the return is omitted: that is, what you spent, and this is a statement of a general ruling that includes every acceptable and unacceptable charity and every acceptable or unacceptable vow. And his statement: then God knows it contains the meaning of a promise to whoever spends and vows in an acceptable manner, and a threat to whoever does the opposite. The pronoun is unified, although it refers to two things, which are spending and vowing, because the estimate is: And whatever you spend of spending, God knows it, or whatever you vow of vow, God knows it, then one of them was deleted because the other is sufficient, as Al-Nahhas said. It was said: That which was for conjunction with the word or as in your saying: Zaid or Amr, then it is said: I honored him and not: I honored her, and it is better to say: that conjunction with or allows for both matters, unifying the pronoun as in this verse, and in the saying of God the Almighty: And when they see a transaction or amusement, they disperse to it. And His saying: And whoever earns a sin or a crime and then throws it at an innocent person, and its dual as in the saying of God the Almighty: Whether he is rich or poor, God is more worthy of both of them. And among the first in conjunction with the waw is the saying of Imru’ al-Qais: It is clear that the drawing of the Qur’an has not been erased because of its weaving from the south and north. And from it the poet said: We are satisfied with what we have and you are satisfied with what you have, but the opinion differs And from it: And those who hoard gold and silver and do not spend it. It was said: If the pronoun is found after mentioning two or more things, then it is interpreted as mentioned: that is, God knows what is mentioned, and Ibn Atiyyah was certain of this and Al-Qurtubi preferred it and many grammarians mentioned its meaning in their writings. His statement: And the wrongdoers have no helpers means that the wrongdoers themselves have no helpers to support them and prevent them from God’s punishment for what they have wronged themselves with. It is better to carry it in generality without specifying what the context indicates: that is, the wrongdoers, whatever the injustice, have no helpers.
2:271: 271- His saying, If you disclose your charitable expenditures, they are good. It was read with a fatha on the noon and a kasra on the 'ayn, and with a kasra on both of them, and with a kasra on the noon and a sukoon on the 'ayn, and with a kasra on the noon and with a concealed vowel on the 'ayn. The grammarians have mentioned four languages for na'am, and this is the one in which it was read. In this there is a kind of detailing of what was summarized in the previous conditional: that is, if you disclose your charitable expenditures, then it is good to disclose them, and if you conceal them, you will receive their recipients from the poor, so concealment is better for you. The majority of the commentators have said that this verse is about voluntary charity, not obligatory charity, so there is no virtue in concealment in it. Rather, it has been said that disclosing them is better. A group said that concealment is better in obligatory and voluntary charity. His saying, And He will remove from you some of your misdeeds. Abu 'Amr and 'Asim read it in the narration of Hafs with a ya' and raising. Al-A'mash, Nafi', Hamzah, and Al-Kisa'i read it with a noon and jazm. Ibn 'Abbas read it with a ta' above it, a fatha on the fa' and jazm. Al-Husayn ibn Ali al-Ja'fi read it with a noon and a nasb on the ra'. Whoever reads it with the nominative, it is conjoined to the position of the sentence that comes as an answer after the fa', or as the predicate of a deleted subject. Whoever reads it with the jazm, it is conjoined to the fa' and what comes after it. Whoever reads it with the nasb, then it is assumed that. Sibawayh said: The nominative here is the good way, and he permitted the jazm with the interpretation that if you conceal it, concealment will be better for you and will expiate, and Al-Khalil said something similar to what Sibawayh said. And the min in his statement: from your bad deeds is for partiality: meaning something from your bad deeds. Al-Tabari reported from a group that it is redundant, and that is according to the opinion of Al-Akhfash. Ibn Atiyyah said: That is a mistake on their part. Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Ali ibn Abi Talib regarding the words of God Almighty: O you who have believed, spend from the good things which you have earned, he said: gold and silver, and from that which We have produced for you from the earth, meaning from grain and fruit and everything upon which there is zakat. Saeed ibn Mansur, Abd ibn Hamid, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi narrated in his Sunan on the authority of Mujahid regarding his words: Spend from the good things which you have earned, he said: from trade, and from that which We have produced for you from the earth, he said: from fruits. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi who authenticated it, Ibn Majah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, al-Hakim who authenticated it, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated on the authority of al-Bara’ ibn ‘Azib regarding his statement: And do not aim towards that which is defective, spending [in charity], he said: It was revealed about us, the Ansar. We were owners of palm trees, and a man would bring from his palm trees according to their abundance or scarcity. A man would bring a qanu or qanuwain and hang them in the mosque. The people of the Suffah did not have food, so when one of them became hungry, he would bring a qanu and hit it with his stick, and the ripe dates would fall and he would eat. There were people who did not desire good, and a man would bring a qanu with husks and chaff in it, and a qanu that had broken, and he would hang it up. So God revealed: “O you who have believed, spend from the good things which you have earned and from that which We have produced for you from the earth. And do not aim towards that which is defective, spending [in charity] while you would not take it [in charity] except with closed eyes.” He said: If one of you were given something similar to what he was given, he would not take it except with closed eyes. And modesty, he said: After that, one of us would bring the best of what he had. Abd bin Hamid narrated on the authority of Qatada who said: It was mentioned to us that a man would have two gardens, and he would look for the worst of them in terms of dates, and give it in charity and mix it with chaff, so the verse was revealed. God criticized them for that and forbade them from it. Abd bin Hamid narrated on the authority of Ja`far bin Muhammad bin Abihi who said: When the Messenger of God (blessings and peace of God be upon him) ordered the Zakat al-Fitr, a man came with bad dates, so the Prophet (blessings and peace of God be upon him) ordered the one who estimated the date palms not to allow it. So God revealed this verse. Abd bin Hamid, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa’i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Daraqutni, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi narrated in his Sunan on the authority of Sahl bin Hanif who said: The Messenger of God (blessings and peace of God be upon him) ordered and said: Who brought this? And whoever brought something, it was attributed to him, so the verse was revealed: And do not give [your children] that which is bad al-Baqarah 2:170. The Messenger of God (peace be upon him) forbade two types of dates from being given in charity: Ja'rur and Habiq. Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Al-Dhiya' in Al-Mukhtara narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas who said: The companions of the Messenger of God (peace be upon him) used to buy cheap food and give in charity, so God revealed the verse, O you who believe. Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Ubaidah Al-Salmani who said: I asked Ali bin Abi Talib about the statement of God the Most High: O you who believe! Spend. He said: This verse was revealed regarding the obligatory zakat. A man would go to the dates and pick them and set the good ones aside, and when the charity giver came, he would give him some of the bad ones. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement, He grants wisdom to whom He wills, that he said: Knowledge of the Qur'an, its abrogating and abrogated, its clear and ambiguous parts, its beginning and end, its lawful and unlawful parts and the like. Ibn Mardawayh narrated on his authority: It is the Qur'an, meaning its interpretation. Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on his authority that it is the prophecy. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on his authority that he said: It is understanding the Quran. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Abu Al-Darda’ that He gives wisdom means reading the Quran and thinking about it. Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Abu Al-Aaliyah that he said: It is the Book and understanding it. He also narrated on the authority of Al-Nakha’i something similar. Abd Ibn Hamid and Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Mujahid that he said: It is the Book, He gives its accuracy to whomever He wills. Abd Ibn Hamid narrated on his authority that he said: It is accuracy in speech. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Abu Al-Aaliyah that he said: It is the fear of God. He also narrated on the authority of Matar Al-Warraq something similar. Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Saeed Ibn Jubayr something similar. Abd Ibn Hamid, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Mujahid regarding his statement: Then God knows it that he said: He counts it. It has been proven from the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) in the Sahih and other books what is well known, such as his saying (peace and blessings of God be upon him): There is no vow to disobey God, and his saying: Whoever vows to obey God, let him obey Him, and whoever vows to disobey Him, let him not disobey Him, and his saying: A vow is that by which God’s face is sought. And it has been proven from him in the expiation of a vow what is well known. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding his saying: If you disclose your charitable expenditures, they are good, the verse, he said: So he made the secret voluntary charity seventy times better than its public expenditures, and he made the public obligatory charity twenty-five times better than its secret expenditures. And likewise with all obligatory and voluntary acts in all things. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas regarding his saying: If you disclose your charitable expenditures, the verse, he said: This was done before the revelation of Bara’ah, but when Bara’ah was revealed with the obligatory charitable expenditures and their details, the charitable expenditures ended with it. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: If you disclose your charitable expenditures the verse, he said: This is abrogated. And his statement: In their wealth is a recognized right * For the beggar and the deprived he said: It is abrogated. Every charity in the Qur’an was abrogated by the verse in Surat At-Tawbah Alms are only for the poor and there are authentic hadiths attributed to the Prophet about the virtue of secret charity.
2:272: His statement: 272- You are not responsible for their guidance meaning it is not your duty to make them guided and accepting what they are commanded and forbidden from but God guides whom He wills guidance that leads him to what is required, and this sentence is parenthetical and contains a shift, and the reason for which it was revealed will be explained, and what is meant by his statement: of good is everything that is true to the name of good, whatever it may be, and it is related to something omitted: meaning whatever you spend, whatever it may be of good, then he explained that the spending that is considered acceptable is only what is seeking the face of God, the Most High: meaning seeking the face of God. And his statement: will be paid back to you meaning: its reward and recompense in the manner previously mentioned of doubling.
2:273: His statement: 273- For the poor is related to his statement: And whatever you spend of good or to something omitted: meaning, make that for the poor or the predicate of an omitted subject: meaning, your spending for the poor who are restricted in the way of God through conquest or jihad, and it was said: they refrained from earning because of the weakness in it They are unable to travel in the land to earn money through trade and agriculture, and the like because of their weakness, it was said: they are the poor in description, and it was said: everyone who is described by poverty and what was mentioned with it. Then the Almighty mentioned from the conditions of those poor what necessitates compassion and mercy for them, and they are that they are too abstaining from asking from the conditions of those poor what necessitates compassion and mercy for them, and they are that they are too abstaining from asking and showing poverty to the point that the ignorant one thinks they are rich. Ta'tafafu is a verb that is an exaggeration of the verb 'afa 'an al-shay' to refrain from something and refrains from seeking it. There are two pronunciations for yahabshum: opening the seen and breaking it. Abu Ali al-Farsi said: opening is more correct, because the 'ayn of the past tense is broken, so its rule is to come open in the present tense. So reading with the kasra on this basis is good even if it is irregular. The word min in his saying: from ta'tafafu is for the beginning of the goal, and it was said: to clarify the type. His saying: You will recognize them by their mark means by the shabbiness of their clothes and the weakness of their bodies and everything that indicates poverty and need. The address is either to the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, or to anyone who is suitable for addressing. The mark is shortened, and it may be extended. Al-Ilhaaf is insistence in asking, and it is derived from al-lihaaf, and it was named thus because it includes the aspects of asking in asking, just as al-lihaaf includes covering. The meaning of his saying: They do not ask people insistently is that they do not ask them at all, neither a question of insistence nor a question other than insistence. Al-Tabari and Al-Zajjaj said the same, and the majority of commentators agreed with it. The reason is that self-restraint is a fixed characteristic of theirs that does not leave them, and merely asking contradicts it. It was said: What is meant is that if they ask, they ask gently and do not insist in their asking. Although this is what is apparent from the direction of the negation to the restriction rather than the restricted, the characteristic of self-restraint contradicts it. Also, the fact that the ignorant person thinks that they are rich does not happen except with the absence of asking at all.
2:274: And his saying: 274- By night and by day indicates the increase of their desire to spend and the intensity of their keenness on it to the point that they do not leave it by night or by day, and they do it secretly and openly when the need of the needy befalls them, and the poverty of the needy becomes apparent to them at all times and in all circumstances. And the entry of the fa in the predicate of the relative pronoun, I mean his saying: Then they will have their reward is to indicate the causality of what precedes it for what follows it, and it was said: It is for conjunction and the predicate of the relative pronoun is omitted: meaning, and among them are those who spend. Abd bin Hamid, Al-Nasa'i, Al-Bazzar, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Al-Tabarani, Al-Hakim who authenticated it, Al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, and Al-Dhiya' in Al-Mukhtara narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: They were reluctant to give charity to their polytheist relatives, so this verse was revealed: You are not responsible for their guidance until His saying: And you will not be wronged, so they were permitted. Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Al-Dhiya' narrated on his authority that he said: The Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) used to command us not to give charity except to the people of Islam until this verse was revealed, then he commanded charity after it to everyone who asked you from every religion.
