It was said that the secret is what a person conceals in himself, and what is even more hidden than that is what was not and no one concealed it. It was said that the secret is the secret of creation, and what is even more hidden than that is the secret of God, the Almighty. Ibn Jarir denied this and said: What is even more hidden is what is not in a person's secret and will be in his soul.
20:8: Then he mentioned that the one described with worship in the aforementioned manner is God, the Most High, the One who is free from any partner and who deserves to be called by the most beautiful names, so he said: 8- “God, there is no god but He. To Him belong the most beautiful names.” So God is the predicate of a deleted subject: that is, the one described with these perfect attributes is God, and the phrase there is no god but He is a new sentence to clarify the exclusive divinity of Him, the Most High: that is, there is no god in existence but Him. And likewise the phrase to Him belong the most beautiful names clarifies His, the Most High, deserving of the most beautiful names, which are the nine and nine mentioned in the authentic hadith. It was previously explained in the words of God Almighty: And to God belong the best names in Surat Al-A’raf. Al-Husna is the feminine of Al-Ahsan, and Al-Asma is the subject and its predicate is Al-Husna. It is possible for God to be the subject and its predicate is the sentence that follows it, and it is possible for it to be a substitute for the pronoun in Ya’lam.
20:9: Then the Almighty decided the matter of monotheism by mentioning the story of Moses, which includes the amazing power and the strange report, so He said: 9- And has the story of Moses come to you? The question is for confirmation, and its meaning is: Has not the story of Moses come to you? It was said that its meaning is: The story of Moses has come to you. Al-Kalbi said: The story of Moses had not come to him at that time. In the context of this story, there is consolation for the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, for what he encounters of the hardships of the rulings of prophethood, and bearing its burdens and enduring its trials, and that this was the case of the prophets before him. What is meant by the hadith is the story that happened to Moses.
20:10: And 10- When he saw a fire is a circumstance of the hadith, and it was said that the agent in it is understood: that is, remember, and it was said that it is understood later: that is, when he saw a fire, it was such and such, and his vision of the fire was on a dark night when he went out traveling to his mother after asking permission from Shu'aib, so when he saw it, he said to his family, stay and what is meant by family here is his wife, and the plural is for the apparent meaning of the word family or for emphasis, and it was said that what is meant by them is the woman, the child, and the servant, and the meaning of stay is to stay in your place, and he used the word stay without residence because staying requires permanence, and staying is not like that. Hamza read to his family with a damma on the ha', and so on in Al-Qasas. Al-Nahhas said: This is according to the language of the one who said: I passed by him, O man, so he came with it according to the original, and it is permissible, except that Hamza differed from his original in these two places in particular: I perceived a fire, meaning I saw. It is said: I perceived a sound, I heard it, and I perceived a man, I saw him. It was said: Intimacy is clear sight, and it was said: Intimacy is specific to seeing what brings one closer, and the sentence is an explanation of the command to stay, and since the bringing of the torch and the presence of guidance were expected, he explained the command with hope, so he said: Perhaps I will bring you a torch from it, meaning I will bring you a torch from the fire, and the torch is a flame from the fire, and so is the miqbas, it is said: I took a fire from him, I took a torch, so he took me: meaning he gave me, and so is I quoted. Al-Yazidi said: I took knowledge from the man and I took fire from him, so if you sought it for him, you say I took it from him. Al-Kisa’i said: I took from him both fire and knowledge. He said: I also took from him in both of them, ‘or I find guidance on the fire,’ meaning a guide who guides me to the path and directs me to it. Al-Farra’ said: He increased the guide, so he mentioned it in the form of a source, or he expressed it with the source to exaggerate by deleting the complement: meaning one with guidance. The word or in both places is to prevent the emptiness of the plural, and the letter of superiority is to indicate that the people of the fire are superior to the place closest to it.
20:11: 11- So when he came to it, he was called meaning when he came to the fire that he sensed, he was called from the tree, as is stated in Surat al-Qasas 28:meaning from its direction.
20:12: And from its side 12- O Moses, indeed I am your Lord meaning he was called and it was said, O Moses. Abu Amr, Ibn Kathir, Abu Jaafar, Ibn Muhaisin, Hamid and Al-Yazidi read ani with the opening of the hamza. The rest read it with the breaking of it: meaning that I Take off your sandals God the Almighty ordered him to take off his sandals, because that is more expressive of humility, and closer to honor, respect and good manners. It was said that they were made of untanned donkey skin, and it was said that the meaning of taking off the sandals is emptying the heart of family and money, and it is one of the innovations in interpretations. Then God the Almighty explained the command to take them off by saying: Indeed, you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa the sacred and purified, and the holy is purity, and the holy and purified land, it was called that because God expelled the disbelievers from it and populated it with believers, and Tuwa is the name of the valley. Al-Jawhari said: “Tawa is the name of a place in Ash-Sham, with a kasra on the ta’ and a damma. It is declined and not declined. Whoever declines it makes it the name of a valley or a place and makes it indefinite, and whoever does not decline it makes it a town or a spot and makes it definite. Ikrimah read Tawa with a kasra on the ta’, and the rest read it with a damma. It was said that Tawa is like thana from taiy, a source for nawadi, or for al-muqaddas, meaning he was called twice, or sanctified once after another.
20:13: 13- And I have chosen you The people of Medina, the people of Mecca, Abu Amr, Ibn Amir, Asim, and Al-Kisa'i read And I have chosen you in the singular. Hamza read And I have chosen you in the plural. Al-Nahhas said: The first reading is better for two reasons: One of them is that it is more similar to the script, and the second is that it is better in the order of the speech, because of His saying: O Moses, indeed I am your Lord, and the meaning of I have chosen you is that I have selected you for prophethood and the message, and the fa in His saying: So listen to what is revealed is to arrange what comes after it according to what comes before it, and ma is a relative pronoun or a source, meaning so listen to what is revealed to you, or to the revelation.
20:14: And sentence 14- I am God instead of what is in what is revealed. Then He, the Most High, commanded him to worship, saying: Worship Me. The fa here is like the fa before it, because the fact that divinity is exclusive to Him, the Most High, requires that He be singled out for worship. And establish prayer for My remembrance. He singled out prayer for mention, even though it is included in the command to worship, because it is the most honorable obedience and the best worship. He explained the command to establish prayer by saying for My remembrance: that is, so that you remember Me, because complete remembrance is not achieved except within worship and prayer, or the meaning is so that you remember Me in them, because they include remembrances, or the meaning is: establish prayer whenever you remember that you have to pray. It was said that the meaning is: so that I may remind you with praise in the highest place, so the source according to this may be added to the subject or to the object.
20:15: And sentence 15 - The Hour is coming is an explanation of the command that preceded it: meaning that the Hour, which is the time of reckoning and punishment, is coming, so do good deeds by worshipping God and praying. The meaning of I almost hid it is disputed. Al-Wahidi said: Most of the commentators said: I hid it from myself, and this is the opinion of Saeed bin Jubair, Mujahid and Qatadah. Al-Mubarrad and Qutrub said: This is according to the custom of addressing the Arabs, they say: If they go to extremes in concealing something, I hid it even from myself, meaning I did not tell it to anyone. The meaning of the verse is that God went to extremes in concealing the Hour, so He mentioned it in the most eloquent way known to the Arabs. Saeed bin Jubair narrated that he read akhfayha with a fat-ha on the hamza, meaning he revealed it. Abu Ubaidah narrated the same from Al-Kisa’i, from Muhammad bin Sahl, from Wafa’ bin Iyas, from Saeed bin Jubair. Al-Nahhas said: There is no other chain of transmission for this narration. Al-Qurtubi said: Ibn Al-Anbari narrated it the same way in Kitab Al-Radd. He said: My father told me, Muhammad bin Al-Jahm told us, Al-Farra’ told us, Al-Kisa’i told us, and he mentioned it. Al-Nahhas said: Better than this chain of transmission is what Yahya Al-Qattan narrated from Al-Thawri from Ata’ bin Al-Sa’ib from Saeed bin Jubair that he read akhfayha with a damma on the hamza. Ibn al-Anbari said: Al-Farra’ said: The meaning of the reading of the fat-ha is I almost revealed it, from I revealed something if you reveal it, I conceal it. Al-Qurtubi said: Some linguists said: It is possible that I revealed it with a damma on the alif means I revealed it, because it is said I concealed something and I concealed it from the letters of opposites, which are said to cover and reveal. Abu Ubaidah said: I concealed it and I concealed it have the same meaning. Al-Nahhas said: This is good. Al-Farra’ and Sibawayh recited what indicates that the meaning of I revealed it is I revealed it, and that is the saying of Imru’ al-Qais: If you conceal the disease, we will not fear it, and if you start a war, we will not sit back. Meaning: If you conceal the disease, we will not reveal it. Abu Ubaidah narrated on the authority of Abu al-Khattab that it is with a damma on the nun from nakhfa, and Imru’ al-Qais said: He concealed them from their tunnels, as if he had stepped on them and was delicate from the claws of his feet. That is: their most apparent. An-Nahhas falsified this statement and said: The meaning is not on the most apparent, especially since the most hidden of them is an anomalous reading, so how can the correct and common reading be rejected? Ibn al-Anbari said: There is another interpretation of the verse, which is that the speech is cut off at almost, and he considers it implied: that is, I almost bring it, and the beginning occurred with the most hidden of them so that every soul may be rewarded for what it strives for, and similar to it is the statement of Umair ibn Dabi’ al-Barjami: I intended to do it but did not, and I almost did. I wish I had left Uthman's wives crying over him. I almost did, and this is the copper chosen. Abu Ali Al-Farsi said: It is from the category of negation and not opposites, and the meaning of hid it: I removed its concealment, which is its covering, and from this is their saying I complained to him: meaning I removed his complaint. Abu Hatim narrated from Al-Akhfash that akada is redundant for emphasis, he said: And similar to it - if he puts out his hand he can hardly see it - and similar to it is the saying of the poet: Quick to attack, he sharpens his weapon, and his horn barely breathes. He said: The meaning is that I almost concealed it: that is, I almost did it, because if you say: Zayd almost stood up, it is possible that he stood up or that he did not stand up, and the evidence that he concealed it is indicated by the evidence of other than this verse on this, and his saying: So that every soul may be rewarded for what it strives for is related to coming or to what it concealed, and what is a source: that is, so that every soul may be rewarded for its striving, and striving, although it is apparent in actions, here it includes actions and omissions, to definitively state that the one who abandons what is required of him is punished for abandoning it and is taken by it.
20:16: 16- So let not those who do not believe in it turn you away from it meaning let not those who do not believe in it turn you away from believing in the Hour, or from remembering it and observing it so that you may not turn away from it from the disbelievers. Although this prohibition is for the disbeliever according to appearance, it is in reality a prohibition for him, may God bless him and grant him peace, from turning away, or from showing leniency to the disbelievers, so it is from the category of: I do not see you here, as is well known. It was said that the pronoun in from it refers to the prayer, and this is far-fetched. His statement: and follows his desire is conjoined with what precedes it: meaning those who do not believe, and those who follow their desire: meaning the desire of their soul by being exhausted in fleeting sensual pleasures so that you will perish meaning that you will be destroyed, because your turning away from it due to the turning away of the disbelievers from you necessitates destruction and entails it. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, Al-Bayhaqi in Al-Shu`ab and Ibn Asakir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas that the first revelation to come down to the Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) was that he would stand on the balls of his feet when he prayed, then God revealed, “Ta-Ha. We have not sent down the Qur’an upon you to make you miserable.” Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated on his authority that he said: They said, This man has been made miserable by his Lord. So God revealed this verse. Ibn Asakir also narrated on his authority that he said: When the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) got up at night, he would tie himself with a rope so that he would not sleep, then God revealed this verse. Al-Bazzar narrated on the authority of Ali that he said: The Prophet (peace and blessings of God be upon him) would alternate between his feet, standing on each foot until this verse was revealed, We have not sent down the Qur’an upon you to make you miserable. Al-Suyuti classified its chain of transmission as good. Ibn Mardawayh also narrated on his authority a longer version. Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas that he said: The Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) would sometimes recite the Qur’an when he prayed, and he would stand on one foot, then God revealed, Ta-Ha with your feet, We have not sent down the Qur’an upon you to make you miserable. Ibn Abi Hatim, Al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him regarding his statement: Ta-Ha, he said: O man. Al-Harith Ibn Abi Usamah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Abbas, who said: Ta-Ha in Nabataean means O man. Abd Ibn Hamid and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, who said: It is like saying ‘sit down.’ Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him, who said: Ta-Ha in Nabataean means O man. Ibn Jarir narrated from him, who said: Ta-Ha in Syriac means O man. Al-Hakim also narrated from him, who said: Ta-Ha is like saying: O Muhammad in the Ethiopian language. There are differences and contradictions in these narrations from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Tufayl, who said: The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: I have ten names with my Lord. Abu Tufayl said: I have memorized eight of them: Muhammad, Ahmad, Abu al-Qasim, al-Fatih, al-Khatim, al-Mahi, al-‘Aqib, and al-Hashir. Sayf claimed that Abu Ja’far told him: The two remaining names are Ta-Ha and Ya-Seen. Al-Bayhaqi narrated in Al-Dala'il on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: "Ta-Ha. We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to make you miserable." He said: O man, We have not sent down the Qur'an to you to make you miserable. And he used to stand at night on his feet, so it is a language for 'Ak. If you say to 'Akki, O man, he does not turn around, and if you say Ta-Ha, he turns around to you. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: Ta-Ha is an oath by which God swears, and it is one of His names. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Qatada regarding his statement: And what is beneath the soil, he said: Soil is everything that is wet. Abu Ya'la narrated on the authority of Jabir, "The Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was asked: What is beneath this earth? He said: Water. It was asked: What is beneath the water? He said: Darkness. It was asked: What is beneath the darkness? He said: Air. It was asked: What is beneath the air? He said: Soil. It was asked: What is beneath the soil? He said: The knowledge of the created is cut off at the knowledge of the Creator." Ibn Mardawayh narrated something similar to it, but longer. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma’ wa’l-Sifat narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement, He knows the secret and what is more hidden, that he said: The secret is what the son of Adam keeps secret in himself, and He conceals what is hidden from the son of Adam of what he will do before he knows it, for He knows all of that in the past and what remains with one knowledge, and all of creation with Him in that is like one soul, and it is like His statement, He did not create you and resurrect you except as one soul. Al-Hakim narrated and authenticated it on his authority regarding the verse, that he said: The secret is what you know, and what is more hidden is what God has cast into your heart of what you do not know. Abdullah bin Ahmad narrated it in Zawa’id al-Zuhd, Abu al-Shaykh in al-Azmah, and al-Bayhaqi with the wording, He knows what you conceal in your soul and He knows what you will do tomorrow. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement, Or I find guidance upon the Fire, that he said: Someone who guides to the path. Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Abd bin Hamid, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ali regarding his statement, Then take off your shoes, that he said: They were made of the hide of a dead donkey, so he was told to take them off. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, You are in the sacred valley of Tuwa. Al-Mubarak said, Tuwa is the name of the valley. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority, In the sacred valley of Tuwa, meaning the holy land, because he passed by its valley at night and Tawa. It is said, I folded the valley of such and such. Ibn Jarir also narrated on his authority, regarding his statement, Tawa, that he said, The valley folded. In the two Sahihs and others, on the authority of Anas, that the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said, If any one of you sleeps through a prayer or forgets it, let him pray it when he remembers it, for God said, ‘Establish prayer for My remembrance.’ At-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Hibban, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said, the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said, Whoever forgets a prayer, let him pray it when he remembers it, for God said, ‘Establish prayer for My remembrance.’ Ibn Shihab used to recite it for remembrance. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, regarding his statement, I almost conceal it, that he said, I do not reveal it to anyone but Me. Saeed bin Mansour, Abd bin Hamid, Ibn Al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, who said: I almost hide it from myself.
20:17: His saying: 17- "And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?" Al-Zajjaj and Al-Farra' said: That is an incomplete noun connected to "by your right hand": meaning what is in your right hand? It was narrated from Al-Farra' that he said: That means this, and if he had said "what is that" it would have been permissible: meaning what is that thing? And the Kufians said the first. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of Moses' question about what was in his hand of the staff was to alert him to it so that the miracle would occur with it after confirming it and contemplating it. Al-Farra' said: The purpose of the question is to confirm the matter so that Moses would say it is my staff to establish the argument against him after he confessed, otherwise God knew what it was in eternity, and the position of "what is the nominative case as a subject, and that is its predicate, and by your right hand is in the accusative case as a state if that is a demonstrative pronoun as is apparent in the wording, and if it is a relative pronoun, then by your right hand" is a relative clause.
20:18: 18- He said, 'It is my staff.' Ibn Abi Ishaq read 'asi' in the dialect of Hudhayl. Al-Hasan read 'asai' with a kasra on the 'ya' because of the meeting of two sukoon letters. Atuka'a 'alayhi means I lean on it when walking and I depend on it when tired and standing. From this comes leaning. And I beat with it my sheep. He beat with the stick, beating with it: if he hits the tree with it so that the leaves fall from it. The poet said: I beat my sheep with a stick because of the softness of their hips and humps. Al-Nakha’i read ahs with a silent s, which means to drive away sheep. This is how Ikrimah read it. It was said that they are two languages with one meaning: And I have other needs in it, meaning needs. The singular is ma’ribah, “ma’ribah,” and ma’ribah with a triangular ra. This is what Ibn al-A’rabi and Qutrub said. He mentioned the details of the benefits of the stick, then followed it with a summary. Some people have enumerated the benefits of the stick, and they mentioned some of them: including the saying of some Arabs: My stick, I set it up for my prayers, and I prepare it for my equipment, and I drive my beast with it, and I strengthen myself with it on my journey, and I lean on it in my walking, so that my steps are wide, and I jump with it the river, and it protects me from stumbling, and I throw my cloak on it, so it protects me from the heat, and warms me from the cold, and it brings me close to what is far from me, and it carries my bag, and the strap for my container, I use it to stand when striking, and I knock with it on doors, and I protect myself with it from the rabid dogs, and it replaces the spear in stabbing, and the sword when dueling with peers, I inherited it from my father and my children will inherit it after me. I came across a nice book in a nice volume on the benefits of the stick by some of the later scholars. He mentioned in it report, poems, nice benefits and elegant jokes. God Almighty gathered for Moses in his stick great proofs and powerful signs by which he was safe from the tricks of magicians and the humiliation of the obstinate. Solomon used it for his sermons, his exhortations and the length of his prayers. Ibn Masoud was the owner of the Prophet’s stick, may God bless him and grant him peace, and his goat. He used to deliver sermons with the stick, as did the caliphs after him. It was the custom of the Arabs to take the stick and lean on it when speaking, in gatherings and sermons.
20:19: 19- He said, ‘Throw it down, O Moses.’ This is a new sentence in response to an implied question. God Almighty commanded him to throw it down to show him the apparent miracle He had made for him in it.
20:20: 20- "So he threw it Moses on the ground and behold, it was a serpent, scurrying" This was by God Almighty changing its descriptions and characteristics until it became a serpent, scurrying: that is, it walked quickly and lightly. It was said that it was a stick with two branches, but the two branches became a mouth and the rest of it became the body of a serpent that moved from place to place and swallowed stones despite its great mass and terrible appearance. So when he saw it like that, he was afraid and terrified and turned away and did not look back.
20:21: Then 21- "He said Glory be to Him Take it and do not fear. We will return it to its former state." Al-Akhfash and Al-Zajjaj said: The estimate is its state, like: "And Moses chose his people." He said: It is permissible for it to be a source, because the meaning of "We will return it is We will make it walk." It is permissible for the source to be in the sense of the active participle: meaning walking, or in the sense of the passive participle: meaning walking. The meaning is: We will return it after you take it to its first state, which is the tyranny. It was said that when it was said to him, "Do not fear," he reached such a state of not being afraid that he would put his hand in its mouth and grab its beard.
20:22: 22- And put your hand to your side Al-Farra and Al-Zajjaj said: The man's side is his arm. Qatrub said: The man's side is his side. He referred to the side as the wing because it is in the place of the wing. It was said that to means with. That is, with your side. The answer to the command is It will come out white meaning your hand will come out while it is white. The place of without evil is the accusative case as a state: meaning without evil, and evil is a defect. He used it as a metaphor for leprosy: meaning it will come out white, its light shining brightly at night and during the day like the light of the sun without leprosy. The accusative case of another sign is also a state: meaning another miracle other than the staff. Al-Akhfash said: Verily, a sign is accusative as a substitute for white. Al-Nahhas said: It is a good statement. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is We have given you or We will give you another sign because when He said It will come out white it indicated that He had given him another sign.
20:23: Then the Almighty explained that by saying: 23- To show you some of Our greatest signs. It was said that the meaning is: We did that to show you, and some of Our signs is related to an omitted word that occurred as a state, and the meaning of the word great is the greatest, and it is an attribute of an omitted described word, and the meaning is: To show you some of Our greatest signs: that is, to show you with these two signs, meaning the hand and the staff, some of Our greatest signs, so it is not necessary for the hand to be the greatest sign alone in order for it to be greater than the staff, so the response to that is that there was nothing in the hand except the change in color only, unlike the staff, for in it, along with the change in color, there is an increase in size, the creation of life, and the ability to do extraordinary things.
20:24: Then the Almighty stated the intended purpose of these miracles, saying: 24- Go to Pharaoh, and He mentioned him specifically because Pharaoh was subordinate to him. Then He explained that by saying: He has transgressed, meaning he disobeyed, was arrogant, disbelieved, was tyrannical, and exceeded the limit.
20:25: And sentence 25 - He said, 'My Lord, expand my chest for me' is a resumption of the answer to an implied question, as if it was said, so what did he say? The meaning of expanding the chest is expanding it. He, peace be upon him, supplicated to his Lord and showed his helplessness by saying: And my chest is constricted and my tongue does not speak freely.
20:26: 26- And make my task easy for me. The meaning of making a task easy is making it easy.
20:27: 27- And untie the knot from my tongue meaning the foreignness that was in it from the burning coal that was thrown into his mouth when he was a child: that is, release the knot from my tongue that was in it. It was said that God Almighty removed that knot entirely, as evidenced by His saying: Your request has been granted, O Moses. And it was said that it did not all go away because He did not ask to untie the knot from his tongue completely, rather He asked to untie a knot that prevented understanding, as evidenced by His saying: from my tongue meaning that it was from the knots of my tongue. This is supported by His saying: He is more eloquent than I in speech, and His saying, narrating from Pharaoh: And he could hardly make himself clear.
20:28: And the answer to the command is his saying: 28- They understand my saying meaning they understand my speech, and jurisprudence in the speech of the Arabs means understanding, then he made it specific to the knowledge of the Sharia and the one who knows it is a jurist, as Al-Jawhari said.
20:29: 29- And appoint for me a minister from among my family.
20:30: 29- And appoint for me a minister from my family, Aaron, my brother. The minister who supports is like the one who eats and eats because he bears the burden of the sultan: that is, his weight. Al-Zajjaj said: Its derivation in the language is from the word wazr, which is the mountain that one takes refuge in to escape destruction, and the minister whose opinion the king relies on in matters and resorts to him. Al-Asma'i said: It is derived from mawazirah, which is assistance, and the word waziran and Harun are in the accusative case as the objects of aj'al, and it was said that its objects are: I have a minister, and Harun is an apposition to the minister, but the first is more apparent, and I have is related to something omitted: that is, being mine, and from my family is an attribute of waziran, and my brother is a substitute for Harun.
20:31: The audience read 31- ashdad with a hamzat wasl.
20:32: And 32- Ashrakhu with a hamzat qata' both in the form of a supplication: meaning O Lord, strengthen me with him and make him my partner in the matter of the message, and the support is strength, it is said azrahu: meaning strengthen him, and it is said back: meaning strengthen my back with him. Ibn Amir, Yahya bin Al-Harith, Abu Haywah, Al-Hasan and Abdullah bin Abi Ishaq read ashdud with a hamzat qata' and ashrakhu with a damma on the hamza meaning I strengthen my support with him and I make him a partner in my matter. An-Nahhas said: They put the two verbs in the place of jazm in response to his saying make for me a minister, and Ibn Kathir and Abu Amr read with a fatha on the ya' of akhy
20:33: 33- So that we may praise You abundantly.
20:34: 34- So that we may glorify You much * and remember You much. This glorification and remembrance are the purpose of the supplication that preceded, and what is meant here is glorification with the tongue, and it was said that what is meant by it is prayer, and the accusative of much in both places is that it is an attribute of a deleted source, or for a deleted time.
20:35: 35- Indeed, You were All-Seeing over us. All-Seeing is the one who sees, and All-Seeing is the one who knows the hidden aspects of things, and this is what is meant here: that is, You were All-Seeing over us when we were young, so You were good to us, so be good to us now as well. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding the staff of Moses, he said: An angel gave it to him when he went to Madyan, and it would give him light at night, and he would strike the ground with it and plants would grow for him, and he would brush leaves with it for his sheep. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ikrimah regarding his statement: And brush leaves with it for my sheep, he said: I would strike the trees with it and the leaves would fall on my sheep. Something similar to this was narrated on the authority of a group of the Salaf. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of his statement: And I have therein needs, he said: Needs. Ibn Abi Shaybah, Abd ibn Hamid, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar on the authority of Mujahid. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated something similar on the authority of al-Suddi. He also narrated on the authority of Qatada, he said: It would give him light at night, and it was the staff of Adam, peace be upon him. And he also narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: So he threw it down, and behold, it was a serpent, darting about. He said: It had not been a serpent before that, so it passed by a tree and ate it, and passed by a rock and swallowed it, and Moses began to hear the sound of the rock in its belly, so he turned and fled, and it was called: O Moses, take it, but he did not take it. Then he was called a second time: Take it and do not fear, and it was said to him the third time: You are among those who are safe, so he took it. And Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority: We will restore it to its former state. He said: Its first state. And they also narrated on his authority: Without harm, he said, without leprosy. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement, And appoint for me a helper from my family, Aaron, my brother, he said: He was older than Moses. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority regarding his statement, And let him share in my task, he said: Aaron was given a prophethood at that time when Moses was given a prophethood.
20:36: When Moses asked his Lord, glory be to Him, to expand his chest, make his task easy for him, remove the impediment from his tongue, and appoint for him a minister from among his people, God, glory be to Him, informed him that He had answered that supplication, and said: 36- Your request has been granted, O Moses, meaning you have been given what you asked for. The question that is being asked for is: that is, what is wanted, like saying: report with the meaning of informed, and the addition of his saying O Moses is to honor him with the address while taking into account the pauses.
20:37: And sentence 37- And We have certainly bestowed favor upon you another time is a renewed statement to strengthen Moses' heart by reminding him of God's favors upon him, and favor is kindness and favor. The meaning is: And We have certainly bestowed favor upon you another time before this time, which is God Almighty's protection of him from the evil of his enemies as He Almighty explained here, and another is another feminine meaning other.
20:38: 38- When We revealed to your mother what is revealed meaning from Us at that time, which is the time of revelation. So if is an adverb for revelation, and what is meant by revelation to her is either mere inspiration to her or in a dream, such that He showed her that or on the tongue of a prophet or on the tongue of an angel, not by way of prophecy like the revelation to Mary or by the previous prophets informing her of that and the report reached her, and what is meant by what is revealed is what will come of the matter to her, He made it ambiguous at first and explained it at second, to magnify its importance.
20:39: And the sentence 39 - Throw him into the chest is explained because the revelation contains the meaning of saying, or it is a source on the assumption that throw him, and throwing here means throwing: that is, throw him into the chest, and the chest was explained in the cow in the story of Talut throw him into the sea that is, throw him into the sea, and the sea is the sea or the great river. Al-Farra’ said: This is an order in which there is recompense: that is, throw him, and he will throw him into the sea, on the shore. The order to the sea is based on placing him in the position of someone who understands and distinguishes, since throwing him on the shore is an order that must happen, and the shore is the seashore, it was called a shore because the water dragged it, Ibn Duraid said. What is meant here is what is next to the shore of the sea, not the shore itself. All of these pronouns refer to Moses, not to the Ark, even though he was thrown with him, but what is meant is Moses, with the pronouns before and after this referring to him. The phrase an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his will take him is the answer to the order to throw him, and what is meant by the enemy is Pharaoh, for when Moses’ mother threw him into the sea, which is the well-known Nile, and a river flowed from it to Pharaoh’s house, God led him in that river to his house, so he took the Ark and found Moses in it. It was said that the sea threw him on the shore, and Pharaoh saw him and ordered someone to take him. It was said that Pharaoh’s daughter found him, and the first is more appropriate. And I bestowed upon you love from Me, that is, God bestowed upon Moses a love from Him, the Most High, in the hearts of His servants that no one sees except Him. I love him, and it was said that He put on him a touch of beauty that no one sees except that he loves him. Ibn Jarir said: The meaning is: And I have bestowed upon you My mercy. It was said that the word min is related to al-qatīta, so the meaning is: I have bestowed upon you love from Me, meaning I have loved you, and whoever God loves, people love him. And that you be made under My eyes means that you be raised and nourished in My sight. It is said that a man made his slave girl, meaning that he raised her, and made his horse, meaning that he continued to feed it and take care of it. The interpretation of under My eyes, under My eyes is correct. An-Nahhas said: This is well-known in the language, but this does not specify Moses, because all things are in the sight of God. Abu Ubaidah and Ibn Al-Akhbari said: The meaning is that you are nourished by My love and will. You say: I take things under My eyes, meaning under My love. Ibn Al-Anbari said: The eye in this verse means the intention of will and choice, from the Arabs’ saying: So-and-so went to bed under My eyes, meaning under My love. It was said that the lam is related to something omitted: i.e. I did that to make, and it was said that it is related to I threw, and it was said that it is related to what comes after it: i.e. and make, in my sight, your sister’s walking is measured. Ibn al-Qa’qa’ read and you make with a sukoon on the lam as a command, and Abu Nahik read it with a fatha on the ta’. The meaning is: and that your movement and actions be by my will, and in my sight.
20:40: 40- When your sister walked is an adverb for I threw or to make, and it is possible that it is a substitute for When We inspired and his sister's name is Mary "Then she said: Shall I guide you to someone who will take care of him?" That is because she went out to find out about him and found Pharaoh and his wife Asiya looking for a wet nurse for him, so she said to them this: That is, Shall I guide you to someone who will take him into his care and raise him? They said to her: Who is that? She said: My mother. They said: Does she have milk? She said: Yes, the milk of my brother Aaron, and Aaron was older than Moses by a year, and it was said more, so the mother came and he kissed her breast, and he did not accept the breast of a wet nurse other than her, and this is the meaning of So We returned you to your mother and in the Mushaf of Abu We returned you, and the fa is eloquent So that her eye may be comforted Ibn Amir read in the narration of Abdul Hamid from him So that she may be comforted with a kasra on the qaf, and the rest read it with a fatha on it. Al-Jawhari said: He made his eyes content with him, and a man with contented eyes, and his eyes have been contented, he is contented and contented. The opposite ofسخنت, and what is meant by the cow of the eye: the joy of her son returning to her after she threw him into the sea and his separation was difficult for her. And do not grieve means that nothing will happen to her that would spoil that joy from sadness for any reason. If he had meant sadness for the reason that her eye was comforted by its disappearance, he would have preceded the negation of sadness for the comfort of the eye, so this negation of sadness is carried over to what happens for a reason that occurs after that. It can be said that since the waw was for the absolute plural, this carrying was not specific. It was said that the meaning is: And do not grieve, O Moses, for the loss of her compassion, and this is arbitrary. And you killed a soul what is meant by the soul here is the soul of the Copt whom Moses poked and killed him, and his killing was a mistake. So We saved you from the grief meaning the grief that occurred with you from killing him out of fear of the punishment in the afterlife or in this world or both of them. It was said that grief is killing in the language of the Quraysh, and how far removed is this. And We tested you with trials Fitnah can mean a trial, and it means a difficult matter, and everything that a person is afflicted with, and trials may be a source. Like Thabur, Ash-Shakur, and Al-Kafur: meaning, We tested you with a test, and We tried you with a test. It is possible that the plural of fitnah is to omit the consideration of the feminine taa’ like Hujur in Hujrah and Yadwar in Badrah: meaning, We saved you time after time from the trials you fell into that were mentioned before God chose him for His message. Perhaps what is meant by mentioning his salvation from the grief that befell him because of that and his salvation from the trials is to thank him for God’s work for him and to strengthen his heart when he faced what would happen to him with Pharaoh and the Children of Israel. So you remained with the people of Madyan for years. Al-Farra’ said: The meaning of the speech is that We tested you with trials, so you went out to the people of Madyan and you remained for years. Such deletion is common in the revelation, and likewise in the speech of the Arabs, as they often delete from speech if the meaning is known. Madyan is the country of Shu’ayb, and it was eight stages from Egypt. Moses fled to it and stayed there for ten years, which is the longest of the two terms. It was said that he stayed with Shu’ayb for twenty-eight years, ten of which was the dowry of his wife, the daughter of… Shu`ayb, and eighteen years remained with him until he had a son. The letter fa in fal-bataht indicates that what is meant by the aforementioned trials is what happened before his stay with the people of Madyan. Then I came at a predetermined time, O Moses, meaning at a time that was predetermined in My judgment and destiny that I would speak to you and make you a prophet, or at a time in which revelation is sent to the prophets, which is the beginning of forty years, or at a time that I knew from Shu`ayb’s telling you about it. The poet said: He attained the caliphate because it was his destiny, just as his Lord gave Moses destiny. The word then is useful for delay, indicating that his coming, peace be upon him, was after a period of time, due to what happened to him of losing his way and his sheep being scattered and the like.
20:41: 41- And I made you for Myself Making: taking on a craft, which is the good that you do for a person, and the meaning: I made you for My revelation and My message so that you would act according to My will. Al-Zajjaj said: Its interpretation is that I chose you to establish My argument, and I made you between Me and My secret, and you became, by conveying it on My behalf, in the same position that I would be in if I addressed them and argued with them. It was said that it is a representation of the great honor that God Almighty granted him by bringing the king close to some of His special ones.
20:42: 42- Go, you and your brother meaning let your brother go, and this is a new statement introduced to explain what is meant by the fabrication and the meaning of with My signs with My miracles that I made a sign for you, which are the nine signs and do not slacken in remembering Me meaning do not weaken or slacken, it is said wana yanyani wanayan: if he weakens. The poet said: Muhammad has not slept since God forgave him for his past and future sins. Imru Al-Qais said: It flows when the swimmers on the waves raise dust with the assigned iron. Al-Farra’ said: “In My remembrance and about My remembrance are the same. The meaning is: Do not fall short of remembering Me by being kind to you, bestowing favors upon you, and remembering the blessing as thanks for it.” It was said that the meaning of do not be slow is do not be slow in conveying the message. In Ibn Mas’ud’s reading, do not be weak in remembering Me.
20:43: 43- Go to Pharaoh, for he has transgressed. This is an order for both of them to go, and Moses is present and Aaron is absent, giving priority to Moses, because he is the origin of the message. The reason for the order to go is based on his saying: For he has transgressed, meaning he has exceeded the limit in disbelief and rebellion. Moses alone was singled out for the order to go in what came before, and he gathered them together here to honor Moses by singling him out, and to emphasize the order to go by repeating it. It was said that this is evidence that it is not sufficient for one of them to go. It was said that the first is an order for Moses to go to all the people, and the second is an order for them to go to Pharaoh.
20:44: Then He, the Almighty, ordered them to speak to him softly, because that has an effect on the answer, for roughness at the beginning is one of the greatest causes of aversion and stubbornness in disbelief, and soft speech is that in which there is no roughness, it is said: Nothing softens softly, and what is meant is that they left it for the sake of reprimand, like their saying: Would you like to be purified? It was said that soft speech is a nickname for him, and it was said that he would provide him with the pleasures of this world if he answered, then He explained the command to speak to him softly by saying: 44- Perhaps he will remember or fear that they did that directly from those who hope and desire, so hope refers to them as a group of grammarians said: Sibawayh and others. Its investigation has been presented in more than one place. Al-Zajjaj said: Perhaps the word hope and hope are used, so he addressed them with what they understand, and it was said that perhaps here means interrogation. The meaning is: So see if he remembers or fears, and it was said that it means so that. Remembrance: looking at what they have achieved of remembrance and thinking deeply about it until that is a reason for the answer, and fear is the fear of God’s punishment promised on their tongues, and the word or to prevent seclusion without the group. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Al-Suddi regarding his statement: Then cast him into the river, he said: It is the Nile. Abd bin Hamid and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: And I bestowed upon you love from Me, he said: Everyone who saw him, I bestowed love from Him upon him. Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Salamah bin Kuhayl, he said: I made you beloved to My servants. Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Abu Imran Al-Jawni regarding his statement: And that you be brought up before My eyes, he said: He was raised in the eye of God. Abd Al-Razzaq Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Qatada regarding the verse: He said: So that you be fed before My eyes. Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Jurayj regarding the verse: He said: You are in My eyes when your mother placed you in the chest, then in the sea, and when your sister walked. Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Al-Khatib narrated on the authority of Ibn Umar: I heard the Messenger of God (peace and blessings of God be upon him) say: “Moses killed the one who was killed from the people of Pharaoh by mistake. God the Almighty says: ‘And you killed a soul, and We saved you from the distress’ He said: Who killed a soul, ‘And We tried you with trials’ He said: We purified you with purity.” Saeed bin Mansour, Abd bin Humaid, Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: ‘And We tried you with trials’ He said: We tested you with a trial. Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority: He said: We tested you with a test. Abd bin Humaid, Al-Nasa’i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas a long narration explaining the verse, so whoever wants to complete that can look at it in the Book of Interpretation from Sunan Al-Nasa’i. Ibn Jarir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: ‘Then you came at a fixed time’ He said: At a fixed time. Abd bin Humaid, Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Mujahid and Qatadah: ‘At a fixed time’ He said: An appointment. Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, And do not be slow, he said: Do not delay. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ali, regarding his statement, with gentle speech, he said: Its meaning. Abd bin Hamid and Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas, he said: Its meaning. Ibn Al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on his authority, regarding his statement, Perhaps he will be reminded or fear, he said: Will he remember?
20:45: The majority read 45- that he may rush with the opening of the yaa and the damma of the raa, and the meaning of that is: that we fear that he may make and hasten our fall, it is said that he rushed from him an affair: meaning he rushed, and from it is the farit, which is the one who precedes the people to the water: meaning he punishes us with the punishment of the one who rushes in sin, and he is the one who is ahead in it, this is what Al-Mubarrad said. He also said: Farid from him an affair and afarat: he was excessive, and farat: he left. Ibn Muhaisin read yafrut with the damma of the yaa and the fatha of the raa: meaning a carrier compels him to rush to us, and a group read with the damma of the yaa and the kasra of the raa, and among them Ibn Abbas, Mujahid and Ikrimah from the farit: meaning he goes to extremes in harming us. The rajaz poet said: The foreigner has been too harsh on us and hastened. The meaning of or that he becomes arrogant was mentioned earlier.
20:46: And the sentence 46 - He said, 'Do not fear' is a resumption of the answer to an implied question, a prohibition to them from the fear that they had from Pharaoh, then he explained that by saying: Indeed, I am with you meaning with victory for them, and assistance against Pharaoh, and the meaning of I hear and see is the awareness of what is happening between them and him such that nothing is hidden from Him, glory be to Him, and He is not unaware of them.
20:47: Then He ordered them to come to Him, which is an expression for reaching Him after He ordered them to go to Him, so there is no repetition. 47- And say, 'Indeed, we are messengers of your Lord.' We have been sent to you. So send with us the Children of Israel. That is, leave them alone and release them from captivity. And do not torment them. By remaining as they were, they were in severe torment with Pharaoh: he slaughtered their sons, took their women captive, and made them work that they could not bear. Then He, the Most High, ordered them to say to Pharaoh, We have come to you with a sign from your Lord. It was said that it was the staff and the hand. It was said that Pharaoh said to them: What is it? So Moses put his hand in the pocket of his shirt, then he took it out and it had a ray like the ray of the sun. Pharaoh was amazed by that, and Moses had not seen the staff except on the day of adornment. "And peace be upon him who follows guidance." That is, safety. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, whoever follows guidance is safe from the wrath of God, the Almighty, from His punishment, and it is not a greeting. He said: The evidence for that is that it is not the beginning of a meeting or a speech. Al-Farra’ said: Peace be upon he who follows guidance, and to all who follow guidance it is the same.
20:48: 48- Indeed, it has been revealed to us from God Almighty that the punishment is upon whoever denies and turns away. What is meant by punishment is destruction and ruin in this world and eternity in the Fire. What is meant by denial is the denial of God’s signs and His messengers, and turning away is turning away from accepting them and believing in them.
20:49: 49- He said, 'Who is your Lord, O Moses?' That is, Pharaoh said to them: Who is your Lord? So he added the Lord to them and did not add Him to himself because he did not believe them and denied the Lordship. He singled out Moses for the call because he was the origin of the message, and it was said that it was because the heads of the verses matched.
20:50: 50- He said, 'Our Lord is He who gave each thing its form and nature' meaning Moses said in response to him, and Our Lord is the subject, and He is He who gave each thing its form is the predicate. It is possible that Our Lord is the predicate of a deleted subject, and what follows it is its description. The majority read He created it with a sukoon on the lam, and Zaidah narrated from Al-A'mash that he read He created it with a fatha on the lam as a verb, and this is the reading of Ibn Abi Ishaq, and Nasir narrated it from Al-Kisa'i. According to the first reading, He created it is the second object of He gave. The meaning is: He gave each thing its form and shape that matches the benefit assigned to it and matches it, like the hand for gripping, the foot for walking, the tongue for speaking, the eye for seeing, and the ear for hearing. This is what Ad-Dahhak and others said. Al-Hasan and Qatadah said: He gave each thing its goodness and guided it to what is good for it. Mujahid said: The meaning is that He did not create the creation of man in the same way as the creation of animals, nor did He create animals in the same way as the creation of man, but He created everything and determined it with a determination. From this is the saying of the poet: And He has created everything, and likewise God does whatever He wills. Al-Farra’ said: The meaning is that He created for man and woman, and for each male what matches him from the females. It is possible that His creation according to the first reading is the first object of He gave: that is, He gave His creation everything they need and are comfortable with. The meaning of then He guided is that He, glory be to Him, guided them to the ways of benefiting from what He gave them, so they benefited from everything for which He created it. As for the second reading, the verb is an attribute of the noun or the noun it is added to: that is, He gave everything that God, glory be to Him, created and did not leave it without His giving. According to this reading, the second object is omitted: that is, He gave everything that He created what it needs, so its meaning agrees with the meaning of the first reading.
20:51: 51- "He said, 'What is the matter with the former generations?'" When Pharaoh heard what Moses argued with in this speech to prove the Lordship, as is not hidden from the fact that creation and guidance are established without dispute, and they must have a Creator and Guide, and that Creator and Guide is God, the Most High, and there is no Lord other than Him. Pharaoh said: What is the matter with the former generations? They did not acknowledge the Lord to whom you call, O Moses, but rather worshipped idols and similar creatures. The meaning of "bal is state and affair": that is, what is their state and affair? It was said that Pharaoh's question about the former generations was to deceive Moses when he feared that it would appear to his people that he had defeated him with the argument: that is, what is the state of the past generations, and what events happened to them?
20:52: So Moses answered him, so 52- He said, 'The knowledge thereof is with my Lord' meaning that what you asked about is not what we are concerned with, rather it is from the knowledge of the unseen that God has kept to Himself, neither you nor I know it. According to the first interpretation, the meaning of the knowledge thereof is with my Lord is that the knowledge of those who worshipped idols and the like is preserved with God in His Book, and He will reward them for it. The meaning of it being in a Book is that it is recorded in the Preserved Tablet. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is that their deeds are preserved with God, and He will reward them for them. The meaning is: The knowledge of their deeds is with my Lord in a Book. There are different opinions about the meaning of My Lord does not err nor does He forget: The first opinion is that it is the beginning of a speech to glorify God Almighty from these two attributes. The speech was completed when He said in a book, as Al-Zajjaj said. He said that the meaning of does not err is does not perish from His saying Should we then go astray in the earth? "nor does He forget" anything from things, so He glorified Him from perishing and forgetting. The second opinion is that the meaning of does not err is does not make mistakes. The third opinion is that its meaning is does not disappear. Ibn Al-A'rabi said: The origin of error is disappearance. The fourth opinion is that the meaning is that He does not need a book, and the knowledge of any thing does not go astray from Him, nor does He forget what He knows of it. This was also narrated from Al-Zajjaj. Al-Nahhas said: It is the most similar in meaning. It is clear that it is like the statement of Ibn Al-A'rabi. The fifth opinion is that these two sentences are an attribute of the book, and the meaning is that the writer does not depart from God nor does he forget Him.
20:53: 53- "Who made the earth a cradle for you" The relative pronoun is in the nominative case as an attribute of my Lord, including additional clarification. It is also possible that it is the predicate of a deleted subject, or in the accusative case as a compliment. The Kufians read "mahd" as a source for an implied verb: meaning He made it a cradle, or as an implied deleted noun: meaning having a cradle, and it is a name for what is made a cradle like a bed for what is spread out. The rest read "mahadan" and Abu Ubaid and Abu Hatim chose this reading. He said that they agreed on the reading: "Have We not made the earth a cradle?" An-Nahhas said: The plural is more appropriate than the source, because this position is not the position of the source except with the deletion of the noun. It was said that it is possible that it is a singular mahd like a bed, or it is possible that it is a plural, and the meaning of mahd is the mattress, so mahd is the plural of mahd: meaning He made every place in it a cradle for each one of you. "And He made for you paths therein." The path: inserting something into something. Meaning: He has inserted into the earth paths for you to walk on and has made them easy for you. In another verse: Who made the earth a bed for you and made for you paths therein that you may be guided. Then the Almighty said, thanking His servants: And sent down water from the sky. This is rainwater. It was said that Moses’ speech ended here, and what follows is: Then We brought forth thereby pairs of diverse plants. This is from the speech of God the Almighty. It was said that it is from the speech attributed to Moses, in apposition to sent down. Rather, the shift to speaking was made to draw attention to the apparent meaning of what is in it of the indication of the perfection of power. It was discussed that this is contrary to the apparent meaning, as it entails missing the shift due to the lack of unity of the speaker. The answer to this is that the entire speech is attributed to one person, Moses, and the one who narrates all of them is God the Almighty. The meaning: So We brought forth thereby the water, due to cultivation and treatment, pairs: meaning types and similarities of different kinds of plants. His saying of plants is an attribute of pairs, or a clarification of it, and similarly varied is another attribute of it, meaning scattered, the plural of dispersed. Al-Akhfash said: The estimation is different pairs of plants. He said: The plants may be different, so it is possible for different to be an adjective for pairs and it is possible for it to be an adjective for the plants. It is said that a matter is scattered: meaning scattered, and the matter is scattered, and scattered is similar to it, and scattering is dispersed. Ru’bah said: They came together and fell apart.
20:54: And the sentence 54 - "Eat and graze" is in the accusative case as a state with the estimation of the saying: meaning saying that to them, and the command is for permission: it is said the livestock grazed the pasture and their owner grazed it with care: meaning he fed them and let them go. It comes intransitively and transitively, and the reference in his saying: "Indeed in that are signs for those of understanding" is to what was mentioned previously in these verses, and the prohibition is the minds, the plural of prohibition, and those of understanding were singled out because they are the ones who abide by their opinion, and it was said because they forbid the soul from ugly things, and all of this is from Moses as an argument against Pharaoh in proving the Creator in response to his saying: "So who is your Lord, O Moses?"
20:55: The pronoun in 55- "From it We created you" and what follows refers to the earth mentioned previously. Al-Zajjaj and others said: It means that Adam was created from the earth and his children from it. It was said that the meaning is that every sperm created from the dust is included in the creation of Adam, because every individual among the human beings has a share of his creation. "And into it meaning into the earth We will return you" after death, so you will be buried in it and your parts will be dispersed until they become of the same kind as the earth. The word "in came without to" to indicate stability. "And from it meaning from the earth We will bring you out another time" meaning by resurrection and revival and the composition of bodies and the return of souls to them as they were before death, and the time is like the time.
20:56: 56- "And We showed him all Our signs" meaning We showed Pharaoh and made him know all Our signs. What is meant by the signs are the nine signs mentioned in His statement: "And We gave Moses nine signs", with the addition being for the covenant. It was said that what is meant are all the signs that Moses brought, and those that other prophets brought, and that Moses had known all his miracles and the miracles of all the prophets, and the first is more appropriate. It was said that what is meant by the signs are the proofs of God, the Most High, indicating His Oneness. "But he denied and refused" meaning Pharaoh denied Moses and refused to accept his faith. This indicates that Pharaoh's disbelief was disbelief out of stubbornness because he saw the signs and denied them, as in His statement: "And they denied them, while their souls were convinced thereof, out of injustice and arrogance."
20:57: And sentence 57 - "He said: Have you come to us to expel us from our land with your magic, O Moses?" is a resumption of the answer to an implied question, as if it was said: So what did Pharaoh say after this? The hamza is for denial of the signs brought by Moses: that is, you have come, O Moses, to make people think that you are a prophet who they must follow and believe in what you have brought, until you reach that illusion, which is a branch of magic, until you conquer our land and expel us from it. And the cursed one only mentioned expulsion from the land to repel his people from answering Moses, because if it occurred to their minds and was established in their understandings that the consequence of their answering Moses would be expulsion from their homes and homelands, they would not accept his words, nor consider his miracles, nor pay attention to the good he calls for.
20:58: 58- Then we will bring you magic like it. The fa is to arrange what comes after it according to what came before it, and the lam is the one that introduces the oath: meaning, by God, we will confront you with magic like what you have brought, until it becomes clear to the people that what you have brought is magic that a magician can match. So make an appointment between us and you. It is a verbal noun: meaning a promise. It was said that it is a place name: meaning, make for us a known day, or a known place that we will not break. Al-Qushayri said: It is more apparent that it is a verbal noun, and that is why he said: We will not break it, meaning we will not break that promise. Breaking it means that you promise something and do not fulfill it. Al-Jawhari said: The appointment is the promise and the time is the place, and so is the appointment. Abu Ja`far ibn al-Qa`qa`, Shaibah, and al-A`raj read We will not break it in the subjunctive mood as an answer to his saying make. The rest read it with the nominative case as an attribute of a promise: meaning we will not break that promise, neither we nor you. He delegated the appointment to Moses to demonstrate his complete ability to bring about what Moses brought, and the accusative case of a place other than is an implied verb indicated by the source, or as a substitute for a promise. Ibn Amir, Asim and Hamzah read except with a damma on the seen, and the rest read it with a kasra, and they are two languages. Abu Ubaid and Abu Hatim chose the kasra of the seer because it is the high and eloquent language, and what is meant is a level place, and it was said a place that is fair and just between us and you. Sibawayh said: It is said sawa and sawa: meaning fair, meaning fair between the two places. Zuhair said: Show us a plan that does not harm us and treats us equally. Abu Ubaidah and Al-Qutaibi said: It means a middle place between the two groups. Abu Ubaidah recited for Musa bin Jaber Al-Hanafi: Our father had settled in a town between Qais Qais Ghailan and Al-Fazar. And the farz is Saad bin Zaid Manat.
20:59: Then Moses promised him a specific time, so He said, 'Your appointment is on the Day of Adornment.' Mujahid, Qatadah, Muqatil, and As-Suddi said: That was a festival day when they would beautify themselves. Saeed bin Jubayr said: That was the Day of Ashura. Ad-Dahhak said: Saturday. It was also said: New Year's Day. It was also said: The day of breaking the Gulf. Al-Hasan, Al-A'mash, Isa Al-Thaqafi, As-Sulami, and Hiba from Hafs read Day of Adornment in the accusative case. This reading was narrated from Abu Amr: That is, on the Day of Adornment, our appointment will be fulfilled. The rest read it in the nominative case, as a predicate of your appointment. The appointment was made a time after Pharaoh asked him to make it a regular place, because Day of Adornment indicates a famous place where people will gather on that day, or according to the estimation of a deleted complement: That is, your appointment is the place of Day of Adornment. And that the people will be gathered at noon. It is conjoined with Day of Adornment, so it is in the nominative case, or with Adornment, so it is in the genitive case, meaning the morning of that day, and what is meant by the people is the people of Egypt. Meaning: They will be gathered for the Eid at the time of the forenoon, and they will look into the matter of Moses and Pharaoh. Al-Farra’ said: The meaning is, When you see people gathered from every side at noon, then that is the appointed time. He said: It was their custom to gather people on that day. Al-Jawhari said: The forenoon is the forenoon after sunrise, then after it is the forenoon, which is when the sun rises. He specified the forenoon because it is the beginning of the day, so if the matter extends between them, there is plenty of time during the day. Ibn Mas’ud and Al-Jahdari read and that God will gather people at noon in the active form, meaning that God will gather people at noon. It was narrated from Al-Jahdari that he read and that we will gather with a nun and some of the reciters read it with a ta above it, meaning that you, O Pharaoh, were gathered. The rest read it with a ta below it in the passive form. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: Indeed, we fear that he will overpower us, he said: He will hasten, “or that he will transgress,” he said: He will transgress. Ibn al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Jurayj regarding his statement: I hear and I see, he said: I hear what he says and I see what he will answer you with, so it is revealed to you and you will answer it. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Mas’ud who said: When God sent Moses to Pharaoh, he said: My Lord, what should I say? He said: “Say: ‘I am Shara’i.’” Al-A’sha said: The interpretation of that is The Living before everything, and The Living after everything. Al-Suyuti included its chain of transmission, and Ibn Kathir preceded him in authenticating its chain of transmission in his interpretation. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Qatada regarding his statement: Upon whoever denied and turned away, he said: He denied the Book of God and turned away from obeying God. Ibn Al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Al-Bayhaqi narrated in Al-Asma’ wa Al-Sifat on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: He gave each thing its nature, he said: He created for each thing its mate. Then He guided it, he said: He guided it to its place of marriage, food, drink, and dwelling. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: My Lord does not err, he said: He does not make mistakes. Ibn Jarir, Ibn Al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: From diverse plants, he said: Different. And regarding his statement: For those of understanding, he said: For those of piety. Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on his authority: For those of understanding, he said: For those of wisdom and intellect. Abd bin Hamid and Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ata’ Al-Khurasani who said: The angel sets out and takes some of the dust of the place where he is buried and sprinkles it on the sperm, so he is created from the dust and from the sperm, and that is His statement: From it We created you, and into it We will return you. Ahmad and Al-Hakim narrated on the authority of Abu Umamah who said: “When Umm Kulthum, the daughter of the Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace), was placed in the grave, the Messenger of God (may God bless him and grant him peace) said: ‘From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will extract you another time.’ In the name of God, in the path of God, and on the religion of the Messenger of God.” And in a hadith in the Sunan, “He took a handful of dirt and threw it into the grave and said: ‘From it We created you,’ then another and said: ‘And into it We will return you,’ then another and said: ‘And from it We will extract you another time.’” Saeed bin Mansour, Abd bin Hamid and Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated on the authority of Ibn Abbas regarding his statement: Your appointment is on the Day of Adornment, he said: The Day of Ashura. Ibn Al-Mundhir narrated something similar on the authority of Ibn Amr.
20:60: His saying: 60- So Pharaoh turned away meaning he left that place to prepare what he needed from what they had agreed upon. It was said that the meaning is he turned away from the truth, but the first is more appropriate. So he gathered his plot meaning he gathered what he would plot with from his magic and trickery. What is meant is that he gathered the magicians. It was said that they were seventy-two, and it was said four hundred, and it was said twelve thousand, and it was said fourteen thousand. Ibn al-Mundhir said: They were eighty thousand. Then he came meaning he came to the appointment that they had agreed upon with the gathering that he had gathered.
20:61: And sentence 61- Moses said to them is a resumption of the answer to an implied question Woe to you, do not invent a lie against God. He called for woe upon them, and forbade them from inventing lies. Al-Zajjaj said: It is in the accusative case because of an omitted word, and the meaning is that God imposed woe upon them. He said: It is possible that it is a call like his saying: Woe to us who has raised us from our sleep. "He will sweep you away with a punishment." Extortion is eradication. It is said "saht and asaht" mean the same thing, and its origin is the extermination of poetry. The Kufians except Shu'bah read "yashtakum with a damma on the letter of the present tense from asaht", which is the language of Banu Tamim. The rest read it with a fatha from "saht, which is the language of Hijaz and its accusative case as an answer to the prohibition And he who invents has failed" meaning he has lost and perished, and the meaning is: he who invents against God has lost, whatever lie he may have.
20:62: 62- And they disputed their affair among themselves meaning the magicians when they heard Moses' words, they debated, consulted, and exchanged words about that and they whispered secretly meaning from Moses. And their whispering was what they said.
20:63: 63- "These two are magicians." It was said that they whispered among themselves and said: If what Moses brought was magic, then we will defeat him, and if it was from God, then he will have a matter. It was said that what they took prisoner was that if he defeated them, they would follow him. This was said by Al-Farra' and Al-Zajjaj. It was said that what they took prisoner was that when they heard Moses say, "Woe to you, do not fabricate lies about God," they said: This is not the saying of a magician. A secret conversation can be a noun and a source. Abu Amr read "Indeed, these two are magicians with a shaddah on the letter that enters the sentence and with the ya' in the demonstrative pronoun, according to the well-known function of in", which is the accusative of the noun and the nominative of the predicate. This reading was narrated from Uthman, Aisha and other companions. Al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Al-Nakha'i and other followers read it with it. Asim Al-Jahdari and Isa ibn Umar read it with it, as narrated by Al-Nahhas. This reading is in accordance with the apparent i'rab, contrary to the script of the Mushaf, which is written with an alif. Al-Zuhri, Al-Khalil ibn Ahmad, Al-Mufaddal, Abaan, Ibn Muhaisin, Ibn Kathir and Asim, in the narration of Hafs from him, read "Indeed, these two with a shaddah on in", as it is a negative. This reading is in accordance with the script of the Mushaf and the i'rab. Ibn Kathir read like their reading, except that he stressed the noon of "the two". The Medinans, Kufians and Ibn Amir read "Indeed, these two with a shaddah on in" and with an alif, thus agreeing with the script and contrary to the apparent i'rab. A group of scholars have spoken about the interpretation of the reading of the Medinans, the Kufians, and Ibn Amir. Ibn al-Anbari and al-Nahhas have fully mentioned this. It has been said that it is the language of Banu al-Harith ibn Ka’b, Khatham, and Kinanah, who make the dual nominative, accusative, and genitive with the alif. From this, the poet said: He lowered his head like a brave man, and if he could see a way out for us, he would be deaf like a brave man. And the other said: He hit us between the ears And the other said: Her father and her father's father have reached the peak of glory. This is supported by the statement of Sibawayh, Al-Akhfash, Abu Zaid, Al-Kisa’i and Al-Farra’ that this reading is in the language of Banu Al-Harith bin Ka’b. Abu Ubaidah narrated on the authority of Abu Al-Khattab that it is the language of Banu Kinanah, and others narrated that it is the language of Khatham. It was said that an means yes here, as Al-Kisa’i narrated on the authority of Asim, and Sibawayh narrated it likewise. Al-Nahhas said: I saw Al-Zajjaj and Al-Akhfash go with it, so the meaning would be: Yes, these two are magicians. And from this is the saying of the poet: I wonder if there is a cure for the lover’s pain of loving them when they meet Yes, the meeting. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning of the verse is that these two are magicians, then the subject, which is they, was deleted. Abu Ali Al-Farsi and Abu Al-Fath Ibn Jinni rejected this, and it was said that the alif in this is similar to the alif in they do so it was not changed. It was also said that the ha’ is implied: that is, these two are magicians. Al-Zajjaj narrated this from the ancient grammarians, and Ibn Al-Anbari narrated it as well. Ibn Kaysan said: Since this was said with the alif in the nominative, accusative and genitive cases in one case, and the dual does not change the singular, the dual was made the same as the singular, so the alif was fixed in the nominative, accusative and genitive cases. These statements include a correct interpretation of this reading, and it is avoided from error. Thus, what was narrated from Uthman and Aisha, that it was a mistake by the writer of the Mushaf, is dispelled: They want to expel you from your land which is the land of Egypt with their magic which they showed and do away with your best way. Al-Kisa’i said: With your way with your Sunnah. And best is a description like your saying: an elderly woman. The Arabs say: So-and-so is on the best way, meaning on the straight path. Al-Farra’ said: The Arabs say: These are the way of their people and the ways of their people for their nobles. And best is the feminine of best, which is the best. It is said: So-and-so is the best of his people, meaning the best of them, and they are the best. The meaning is: If they are defeated by their magic, the nobles and masters among you will incline towards them, or they will do away with your school of thought which is the best of schools of thought.
20:64: 64- So gather your plan consensus is the rulings, and the determination to do something was said by Al-Farra'. You say I gathered to go out like I resolved. Al-Zajjaj said: Its meaning is let your determination be like the plan agreed upon, and the reciters agreed to cut the hamza in ajma'u except for Abu Amr, who read it by connecting it and opening the meem of the group. Al-Nahhas said: And what was narrated to me from Muhammad bin Yazid Al-Mubarrad is that he said: Abu Amr must read differently from this reading, which is the reading that most people follow. Then come in a row meaning lined up and gathered together so that their affairs are more organized and their awe is greater, and this is the opinion of the majority of commentators. Abu Ubaidah said: The row is the place of the gathering and it is called the prayer place, the row. Al-Zajjaj said: According to this, its meaning is: Then come to the place where you gather for your Eid and your prayers. It is said: I came to the row meaning I came to the prayer place, so according to the first interpretation, the accusative of row is in the state, and according to the interpretation of Abu Ubaidah, its accusative is in the object. Al-Zajjaj said: It is possible that the meaning is: Then come to the people in rows, so it would be a verbal noun in the place of the state, and for this reason it was not collected, and it was read with a kasra over the hamza followed by a ya’, and whoever left out the hamza replaced it with an alif.
